# Welcome, game maker! {.unnumbered #welcome}

::: {.book-hero}

[LEARN BY MAKING]{.eyebrow}

[Web Game Coding for Kids]{.hero-title}

*Learn JavaScript by Building 2D and 3D Games*

**Hung-Fu Chang, Ph.D. and Wenhui Zhu, Ph.D.**

Build a game. Understand the code. Make it your own.

[20 chapters]{.hero-chip} [Visual explanations]{.hero-chip} [Advanced Study]{.hero-chip}

:::

This book teaches JavaScript in the order a young game designer needs it. Instead of memorizing programming rules first, you will meet a problem inside a game and learn the programming idea that solves it.

::: {.callout-tip .big-idea title="The rule of this book" icon="false"}

**Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior.**

First decide what belongs in the game. Next make those parts readable and recognizable. Then give them actions and rules. Use the same thinking strategy for every example, exercise, and challenge.

:::

## Your three-step game-making guide {.unnumbered #sec-development-guide}

Remember **Structure → Style → Behavior**. The full names tell you what to do:

| Step | Ask yourself | What you produce | How to check it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Build the scene structure** | What needs to exist, and how do its parts fit together? | A page or world plan: controls, player, objects, score/status, groups, and starting positions | Point to each required part and explain its job. |
| **2. Style the scene** | How will the player recognize and understand those parts? | Readable layout, colors, shapes, artwork, materials, lighting, and visible feedback | Check visibility, labels, spacing, contrast, and the view of the play area. |
| **3. Program game behavior** | What happens on a player action, a timer tick, or a collision? | Data, operations, actions, rules, and their connections | Predict a result, run or trace the action, and compare the result with your prediction. |

The full names turn the three responsibilities into instructions: **build the structure**, **style**, and **program game behavior**. In the first projects, HTML builds the page, CSS styles it, and JavaScript gives it game actions. In canvas and 3D projects, JavaScript also creates and draws world objects. The steps describe **your design decisions**, not exclusive ownership by a programming language.

A **scene** includes what the player sees and uses: the surrounding page and the game world inside it. A 3D scene object is one part of that larger player-facing scene. **Program game behavior** includes memory, input, movement, rules, timing, and reset—not only animation. **Style** includes readable placeholder shapes; you do not need finished artwork before testing an action.

### Use the guide for every exercise {.unnumbered}

1. **Structure:** identify the parts the task uses. Reuse the current scene, or sketch one for a paper exercise. Add parts only when they are needed.
2. **Style:** check that those parts and their feedback are understandable. Keep the current style when the task changes only a rule.
3. **Behavior:** state the operation or expected result. Write code, trace code, or explain the result, depending on the exercise.

Short reading and prediction exercises can focus on one step. Their **Flow focus** tells you which responsibility you are investigating; it does not ask you to rebuild a game. For challenges, use the concrete **Structure**, **Style**, and **Program game behavior** prompts. Finish with a small check: what did you expect, what happened, and what would you change next?

Repeat the flow for each new feature. A new action may need a new control; return to Structure, style that control, and connect the action. These steps are a development strategy, not the browser's loading order or the game's repeating update-and-draw loop.

## Your computer toolkit {.unnumbered}

Before you make a game, meet the tools you will use. A **computer** runs programs: sets of instructions that tell it what to do. A web browser is one program. A text editor is another. You are about to write instructions that a browser can follow.

### Files and folders {.unnumbered}

A **file** is one named piece of information saved on a computer. A game picture, a sound, and a page of code can each be files. A **folder** is a container that helps you keep related files together. Think of a folder as a game box and the files inside as its cards, pieces, and rule sheet.

Give each game its own folder. For example, your `my-first-game` folder can hold its HTML page now and later hold pictures, sounds, and more JavaScript files. Keep those files together when you copy or move your game.

### A text editor is for code {.unnumbered}

You write code in a **plain-text editor**. It saves exactly the letters, numbers, spaces, and punctuation that you type. Many editors color code and point out mistakes; that can be helpful, but the colors are not part of the code.

A word processor is great for essays, but it may add special quotation marks, hidden formatting, or page layouts. Those extras can confuse code. Use a plain-text editor for your game files. Ask your teacher which editor is available on your computer.

### File names and extensions {.unnumbered}

The end of a file name after the final dot is its **file extension**. It helps people and programs recognize the file's job.

| File name | Extension | What it usually contains |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `index.html` | `.html` | The page structure a browser opens. |
| `main.js` | `.js` | JavaScript instructions for the browser. |
| `style.css` | `.css` | Colors, sizes, and other visual choices. |
| `level.json` | `.json` | Organized game data, such as a level layout. |
| `robot.svg` | `.svg` | A picture made from shapes and lines. |

The extension is important. `index.html` and `index.html.txt` are different files: the first is a web page, while the second is usually treated as ordinary text. Some computers hide extensions, so check the full name when you save a file. Do not rename a file just to give it a new extension; save it in the right kind of file from the start.

## Choose your reading path {.unnumbered}

Follow the main explanations and code examples first. Use the diagrams to trace what the program is doing. Then try a challenge and explain your result in your own words.

Chapters 1-12 establish the web and JavaScript foundations. Chapters 13-16 build a complete 2D adventure. Chapters 17-20 introduce Three.js, custom 3D models, and Rapier physics. The later projects take more time and combine earlier ideas; work through them in small experiments.

Purple **Advanced Study** blocks are optional deeper dives into HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and game systems. They start open; you can collapse them while following the main path and return later.

## What you need {.unnumbered}

- A modern web browser such as Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari.
- A plain-text code editor available on your computer.
- A folder for each website or game containing its files. Chapter 2 begins with separate HTML and CSS files; early JavaScript examples keep their code close to the page so you can focus on the programming ideas.

::: {.callout-tip .setup title="Start with one file" icon="false"}

Create a folder named `my-game-site`. Save your first HTML page as `index.html`, not `index.html.txt`. Open it in your browser. After editing, save the file and refresh the browser. Later, module-based projects need a local development server.

:::

## Meet the browser team {.unnumbered}

Your web browser is the program that turns your game files into a page you can play. Three kinds of code often work together:

| Part | Its job | A game example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **HTML** | Builds the page and names its parts. | A heading, a button, and a canvas. |
| **CSS** | Chooses how those parts look. | A purple button or a large play area. |
| **JavaScript** | Makes the page react and change. | Add a point when the player clicks. |

Use **Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior**: HTML describes the first pages, CSS makes their parts readable, and JavaScript adds game operations and actions. Chapter 2 uses linked HTML and CSS files; Chapter 3 combines a styled scene and JavaScript data in one starter file.

### What “client-side JavaScript” means {.unnumbered}

The **client** is the player's browser. Client-side JavaScript runs on the same computer, tablet, or Chromebook that displays the game. When a player presses a key, the browser can run your JavaScript right there and update the picture right away.

That is different from code on a **server**—another computer that can store shared scores, accounts, or messages. Our first games do not need a server on the internet. Their rules and scores stay in the browser while the page is open.

## Run a one-file game from your drive {.unnumbered}

For the complete examples in the first chapters, you can run your game directly from your computer's drive.

1. Make a folder called `my-first-game` somewhere you can find again, such as Documents.
2. In a plain-text code editor, save the complete example as `index.html` inside that folder. Check that the name ends in `.html`, not `.html.txt`.
3. Open the folder and double-click `index.html`. Your browser should open it. You may see an address beginning with `file:///`; that means the browser opened a file from your own drive.
4. Return to the editor, make one small change, save, and refresh the browser page. On many computers, refresh is `Ctrl+R` or `Command+R`.

If double-clicking opens an editor instead of a browser, right-click the file and choose **Open with**, then choose your browser. If you cannot see the `.html` ending, ask an adult or teacher to turn on file-name extensions. A file named `index.html.txt` is a text document, not a web page.

## When a local web server helps {.unnumbered}

Some later games use several JavaScript files, images, level-data files, or 3D models. A **web server** is a small program that hands files to a browser when the browser asks for them. It is like a careful librarian: the browser asks for a particular file, and the server gives back that file.

For a one-file beginner game, `file:///` is enough. For a project that uses JavaScript `import`, JSON data, or files loaded by the game, start a **local web server** instead. A local server runs only on your own computer and gives the page an address such as `http://127.0.0.1:8000/`. Modern browsers use extra safety rules for those multi-file requests, so opening the HTML by double-clicking may not work.

`127.0.0.1` means “this same computer.” Starting this book's local server does not put your game on the internet or let classmates visit it. The Game Lab instructions in [Appendix E](#sec-game-lab) show exactly how to start it.

## Read examples carefully {.unnumbered}

A **complete example** includes the setup for that small project. A **code fragment** illustrates one part of a game and relies on the variables or functions discussed nearby. Do not paste every fragment into one file without checking where it belongs: some examples replace earlier versions.

Chapters 9–11 use Pong, Breakout, and Snake to explain larger game-building patterns. Each chapter includes a complete small browser example alongside fragments explaining individual rules. Locate its scene, its style, and its actions before changing a fragment. Chapters 13-20 add complete companion projects in the Game Lab. Their chapter snippets explain selected parts; the linked project folders contain the complete runnable source.

## A safe learning habit {.unnumbered}

When a program does not work, do not immediately replace it with someone else's code. Read the browser console, compare one small section at a time, and explain what you expected to happen. Debugging is part of programming, not evidence that you failed.

## Open the Game Lab {.unnumbered}

The companion Game Lab contains six complete projects, including two experimental labs, two collectible adventures, a 3D exploration game, and a model-customization workshop. Keep the project folders together so their shared code and assets can be found.

::: {.callout-tip .setup title="Run the later projects" icon="false"}
From the extracted textbook folder, run `node scripts/serve.mjs`. Open `http://127.0.0.1:8000/games/` in your browser. This local server needs Node.js but no package installation. Use the [Game Lab guide](#sec-game-lab) for controls, file locations, and troubleshooting.

The 2D projects use local files only. The 3D projects initially download pinned Three.js and Rapier modules from a CDN, so they need an internet connection and a browser with WebGL2. An optional dependency-download script supports later offline use.
:::

# Computer, Browser, and Web {#sec-ch01}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[WEB 01 | Before we build a web game]{.game-title}

[Hardware]{.skill-chip} [Software]{.skill-chip} [Browser]{.skill-chip} [Web]{.skill-chip} [URL]{.skill-chip} [Server]{.skill-chip}

:::

## Overview {.unnumbered}

Before you build a web game, it helps to know **where the game lives**, **what runs it**, and **how the pieces reach the screen**.

A web game may look like one thing when you play it, but several parts work together behind the scenes. Your computer provides the hardware. Programs such as a browser provide the software. Files store the pictures, sounds, page information, and game instructions. The Web lets a browser request files from other computers when those files are not already on your own computer.

You do **not** need to memorize every technical word in this chapter. The goal is to build a simple picture in your mind. Later chapters will add HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to that picture one step at a time.

::: {.callout-note title="The big picture" icon="false"}
When you play a web game, you are usually using **software** called a browser on **hardware** such as a laptop or desktop computer. The browser opens game files from your computer or receives them from a server, then uses those files to show and run the game.
:::

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Computer hardware] --> B[Browser software]
    C[Game files] --> B
    B --> D[Web game on the screen]
```

**Read the picture:** The computer is the physical machine. The browser is a program running on that machine. The browser uses files to create the game experience you see.

## Our development flow: Structure → Style → Behavior {#sec-ch01-development-flow}

**Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior.**

The names tell you what to do: **build the structure** by deciding what belongs in the scene, **style** it so the player understands it, and **program game behavior** with operations and actions. Use this thinking strategy whenever you plan a page or game. A **scene** here means the page the player sees: its title, instructions, play area, characters or pictures, controls, and score. First decide what belongs in that scene and how its parts are grouped. Then choose how those parts look. Finally, decide what operations and actions should happen.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[1. Build the scene structure<br/>What belongs on the page?] --> B[2. Style the scene<br/>How should it look?]
    B --> C[3. Program game behavior<br/>What operations and actions happen?]
```

| Development step | Thinking question | Tool and example | Check before moving on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Build the scene structure | What does the player need to see or use? | HTML: a monster button, message, and score area | Each part exists and is in a sensible group and reading order. |
| 2. Style the scene | How can the player recognize and use those parts? | CSS: readable text, spacing, colors, button size | The scene is readable; its controls and play area are easy to find. |
| 3. Program game behavior | What should happen when the player acts or time passes? | JavaScript: remember a score, respond to a hit, move a star | Predict the result of one action, then compare it with the actual result. |

For example, plan **Robot Rescue** in this order: sketch a robot, an arena, a Start button, and a score; choose their sizes and colors; then describe actions such as starting, moving, collecting, and restarting. A drawing on paper is enough to begin the structure step.

This is our **development order**, not a promise about exactly when a browser loads each file. You will return to an earlier step when a new game action needs a new control or display. Build a small scene, style it, add one behavior, and check the result before expanding it.

Chapter 1 helps you plan these three steps. Chapter 2 builds structure and style and writes a behavior plan. Chapter 3 prepares JavaScript memory for the behavior step. Chapter 4 connects that memory to player actions.

## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- use the development flow **Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior** to plan a game;
- distinguish **hardware** from **software**;
- explain the difference between a **program**, a **file**, and a **folder**;
- explain what a **browser** does;
- distinguish the **Internet** from the **Web**;
- distinguish a **web page**, **website**, and **web game**;
- explain what a **URL** is and recognize its basic parts;
- describe the jobs of a **client** and a **server**;
- trace a simple **request and response** between a browser and a server;
- explain the difference between opening a **local file** and visiting a web address;
- describe, at a high level, where a web game can do its work.

## Hardware and software work together

Look at the computer in front of you. You may see a screen, keyboard, mouse, trackpad, and perhaps a desktop computer or laptop case. These are examples of **hardware**.

**Hardware** means the physical parts of a computer system---the parts that are built from electronic or mechanical components. You can usually touch hardware.

Examples include:

- a screen;
- a keyboard;
- a mouse or trackpad;
- a processor;
- memory;
- a storage drive;
- speakers.

Hardware by itself does not know how to open a website or run a game. It needs instructions. Those instructions are provided by **software**.

**Software** is a program, or a collection of programs and data, that tells computer hardware what work to do.

Examples include:

- a web browser such as Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari;
- a text editor used to write code;
- a drawing program;
- a music player;
- a web game running in a browser.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    C[Computer system]
    C --> H[Hardware<br/>physical parts]
    C --> S[Software<br/>programs and instructions]
    H --> H1[Screen]
    H --> H2[Keyboard]
    H --> H3[Storage]
    S --> S1[Browser]
    S --> S2[Text editor]
    S --> S3[Games]
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch Out: A browser is not hardware" icon="false"}
Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari are **software**. The screen that shows the browser is hardware.
:::

### What is a program? {.unnumbered}

A **program** is a set of instructions that a computer can follow. A browser is a program. A calculator app is a program. A game is also a program.

When you start a program, the computer loads the instructions and begins carrying them out. Some programs open documents. Some programs play music. A browser opens and runs web content.

For this book, two programs will be especially important:

- A **text editor** lets you create and change code files.
- A **web browser** reads web files and shows the result.

You will spend a lot of time moving between these two programs: edit something, save it, return to the browser, and see what changed.

## Files and folders keep a project organized

Computers store information in **files**. A file can contain many kinds of information: words, pictures, music, video, data, or program instructions.

A **file name** helps you recognize a file. Many file names also end with a **file extension**, such as `.png` or `.txt`. The extension gives people and programs a clue about what kind of information the file contains.

A **folder** is a container used to organize files and other folders.

Think of a folder as a project box. If you make a space game, you want the files for that game to stay together instead of being scattered around your computer.

```text
space-game/
  index.html
  styles.css
  game.js
  images/
    spaceship.png
    planet.png
  sounds/
    launch.mp3
```

These are real web-project file names. `index.html` describes the page, `styles.css` describes its appearance, and `game.js` holds JavaScript instructions. The name `index.html` is a common starting-page name. An early example may keep all three kinds of code inside one HTML file; a larger project usually separates them.

| File category | Extensions used in this book | Browser's job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Page | `.html` | Read the page structure and find its linked resources. |
| Stylesheet | `.css` | Apply colors, sizes, spacing, and layout rules. |
| Program | `.js` | Run the game instructions. |
| Picture | `.svg`, `.png` | Display an image or use it in a game drawing. |
| Sound | `.wav`, `.mp3` | Load audio that the game can play. |
| Data | `.json` | Read organized information, such as a level layout. |
| 3D model | `.glb` | Supply model data to the later 3D game code. |

The book itself is written in `.qmd` files. **Quarto** turns that manuscript into web pages for reading. When you build a game, you work with the game files above. A browser does not open a `.qmd` chapter as a playable game.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    A[space-game folder] --> B[Page file]
    A --> C[Style file]
    A --> D[Game program file]
    A --> E[images folder]
    A --> F[sounds folder]
    E --> G[spaceship.png]
    E --> H[planet.png]
    F --> I[launch.mp3]
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Try It: Find a file and its folder" icon="false"}
Open a folder on your computer. Pick one file and answer these questions:

1. What is the file's name?
2. Does it have a file extension?
3. Which folder contains it?
4. Which program would you use to open it?
:::

## The Internet and the Web are related, but they are not the same thing

People often use the words **Internet** and **Web** as if they mean the same thing. They are related, but they describe different ideas.

The **Internet** is a huge network that connects computers and devices around the world. It is the communication system that lets connected computers exchange information.

The **World Wide Web**, usually called the **Web**, is a system of pages and other resources that we access through the Internet, usually with a web browser.

One simple way to remember the difference is:

- **Internet:** the network that connects computers.
- **Web:** pages, sites, games, pictures, and other resources that browsers access using that network.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Your computer] --> B[Internet<br/>connects computers]
    B --> C[Web server]
    C --> D[Web pages and game files]
```

The Internet can be used for things other than the Web. The Web is one important service that uses the Internet.

::: {.callout-note title="A useful comparison" icon="false"}
Imagine roads connecting many towns. The **Internet** is like the road system. A **website** is like a place you can reach using those roads. A **browser** is one of the tools that helps you travel to and use that place.

The comparison is not perfect, but it can help you keep the words separate.
:::

## A browser is software that works with web resources

A **web browser** is software that helps you open and use web pages and web applications. Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari are examples.

A browser can get web files in two common ways:

1. It can open files that are already stored on your computer.
2. It can request files from another computer through a network.

After it receives the files, the browser uses them to create what you see and interact with on the screen.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    L[Files on your computer] -->|open| B[Browser]
    B --> S[What you see and use]
    W[Files from a web server] -->|receive| B
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch Out: The browser is not the Internet" icon="false"}
A browser is a program on your device. The Internet is the network connecting devices. You can even use a browser to open some local files when your computer is not connected to the Internet.
:::

### What happens when you type something in the address bar? {.unnumbered}

The long box near the top of a browser is usually called the **address bar**. You can use it to enter a web address. Browsers can also send words from the address bar to a search engine, so typing into the address bar does not always mean that you typed a web address.

When you enter a web address, the browser tries to find the resource at that address. If the resource is on another computer, the browser sends a request for it.

## Web pages, websites, and web games

These three terms are connected, but they do not mean exactly the same thing.

A **web page** is one page or view that a browser can display. A page might show instructions, a menu, a story, a score screen, or part of a game.

A **website** is a collection of related web pages and other files that belong together. A school website, news website, and game website may each contain many pages, images, and other resources.

A **web game** is a game designed to run through a web browser. It may use one page or several files. The browser may draw graphics, play sounds, read keyboard or mouse input, update scores, and run the rules of the game.

| Term | Simple meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Web page | one page shown by a browser | a game's start screen |
| Website | related pages and resources | a game site with a home page, instructions, and games |
| Web game | a game that runs in a browser | a game where you move a character and collect stars |

::: {.callout-note title="Why this matters for our book" icon="false"}
The games in this book are **web games**. That means the browser is not just showing information. It will eventually run instructions that let the game react to clicks, keys, timers, collisions, and other events.
:::

## A URL tells a browser where to look

A **URL** is an address for a resource. URL stands for **Uniform Resource Locator**.

You can think of a URL as directions that help a browser locate something. That "something" might be a web page, an image, a game file, or another resource.

Here is a simple example:

```text
https://example.com/games/space-quest
```

For now, focus on three parts:

| Part | Example | What it tells us |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scheme | `https://` | how the browser should communicate |
| Domain | `example.com` | which site or server name to contact |
| Path | `/games/space-quest` | which resource or location to ask for |

You do not need to memorize every possible URL part yet. The important idea is that a URL gives the browser an address it can use.

::: {.callout-important collapse="true" title="Advanced Study: A URL can contain more parts" icon="false"}
A URL can include additional information. For example:

```text
https://games.example.com:443/levels/maze?mode=easy#start
```

It may contain:

- a **scheme** such as `https`;
- a **host name** such as `games.example.com`;
- an optional **port** such as `443`;
- a **path** such as `/levels/maze`;
- an optional **query** such as `?mode=easy`;
- an optional **fragment** such as `#start`.

You will not need most of these pieces to begin making games. Return to them when a later project needs them.
:::

## Local files and web addresses

A browser does not always need to get a page from the Internet. It can also open a file stored directly on your computer.

A local file address may begin with `file:///`. For example:

```text
file:///Users/your-name/Documents/space-game/start.html
```

The important part is not the exact folder name. `file:///` tells you that the browser is opening a file from the local computer.

A web address often begins with `http://` or `https://`:

```text
https://example.com/games/space-quest
```

That normally tells the browser to contact a server through a network.

| Address begins with | Usual meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `file:///` | open a file stored on this computer |
| `http://` | request a web resource using HTTP |
| `https://` | request a web resource using encrypted HTTP communication |

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    B[Browser]
    L[Local file<br/>on your computer]
    I[Internet]
    S[Web server]
    L -->|open directly| B
    B -->|request| I
    I --> S
    S -->|response| I
    I --> B
```

**Read the picture:** A local file can go directly from storage on your computer to your browser. A web resource takes another route: the browser sends a request through the network and receives a response.

## Client and server describe jobs

When computers communicate, we often describe them by the job they are doing.

A **client** asks for or uses a service or resource. In this book, your browser often acts as a client because it asks for web files.

A **server** provides a service or resource. A web server can receive a request and send back a requested file or other data.

The words **client** and **server** describe roles. They do not always describe special kinds of hardware.

For example, your laptop is hardware. Chrome is software. When Chrome asks a web server for a page, Chrome is acting as a **client**.

A server also involves software. In everyday conversation, people sometimes use the word *server* for both the server program and the computer running that program. For now, remember the job: **a server responds to requests**.

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser (client)
    participant S as Web server
    B->>S: Request a game file
    S-->>B: Send a response
    B->>B: Use the file
```

### Request and response {.unnumbered}

A **request** is a message asking for something.

A **response** is the answer that comes back.

For a web game, a simplified conversation might look like this:

> Browser: "Please send the game page."
>
> Server: "Here it is."
>
> Browser: "Now I need a picture used by the game."
>
> Server: "Here is that picture."

Real web communication contains more details, but this request-and-response idea is the foundation.

## Where does a web game do its work?

A web game can do a lot of work directly inside the browser. For example, the browser can respond when a player presses a key, move an object, update a score, draw graphics, and play sounds.

Some web games also communicate with servers. A server might help with jobs such as:

- saving an online account;
- storing a high score;
- loading shared game data;
- connecting several players.

A beginner game does not need all of those features. Many of the first games in this book can run mostly on your own computer in the browser.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    P[Player] -->|clicks and keys| B[Browser game]
    B -->|updates| G[Game screen]
    B -. optional requests .-> S[Server]
    S -. optional data .-> B
```

::: {.callout-note title="Client-side and server-side" icon="false"}
When work happens in the browser on the player's device, programmers often call it **client-side** work. When work happens in a server program, they call it **server-side** work.

You only need the basic idea now. Most of our early attention will stay on the browser side.
:::

## How HTML, CSS, and JavaScript fit together

You will write HTML and CSS in Chapter 2. First, recognize the three jobs that work together in our games:

- **HTML** describes the page's structure and content.
- **CSS** describes much of the page's appearance and layout.
- **JavaScript** gives the page programmable behavior.

Use them in our development flow: **HTML builds the scene structure → CSS gives it style → JavaScript supplies behaviors**. These three jobs let you build and check a game in manageable stages.

| Technology | Job in a future web game | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HTML | what is on the page | a score area or game button |
| CSS | how it looks | size, spacing, color, position |
| JavaScript | what it does | increase the score after an action |

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    H[HTML<br/>Build the scene structure] --> C[CSS<br/>Style the scene]
    C --> J[JavaScript<br/>Program game behavior]
    J --> G[Web game]
```

Do not worry about the code yet. Chapter 2 begins with HTML and shows how a browser turns page structure into something you can see.

### The browser builds a page from connected files {.unnumbered}

The page file is the starting point. It can point to a stylesheet, pictures, and JavaScript files. The browser loads those resources, builds the page's structure, applies its styles, and runs its scripts. Loading a picture or a program may take time, so later games wait until their resources are ready.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    H[index.html] --> B[Browser builds page elements]
    C[styles.css] --> S[Browser styles the elements]
    B --> S
    S --> P[Page on the screen]
    J[game.js] --> R[Browser runs game instructions]
    R --> P
    A[Pictures, sounds, and models] --> P
```

The browser keeps a working representation of the page called the **Document Object Model**, or **DOM**. A heading, a button, and a score paragraph become elements in that representation. Chapter 2 gives some elements unique labels called **IDs**. Chapter 4 teaches JavaScript to find those elements and change them. Changing the page in the browser does not automatically change the saved HTML file.

### Recognize the page structures we will reuse {.unnumbered}

Our games grow in stages, but they keep familiar page parts: a title, instructions, a play area, controls, and a message or score. The play area changes as we learn new drawing techniques.

| Book stage | Structure to recognize | What HTML and CSS provide | What JavaScript adds |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Chapter 2: static website | Heading, sections, picture, list, player form | Content, labeled controls, a styled card | Game behavior comes later. |
| Chapters 3–5: Monster Clicker | Monster button, message, score paragraph | Visible elements with unique IDs | Chapter 3 stores data; Chapters 4–5 connect clicks and decisions. |
| Chapter 6: Monster Swarm | Container of buttons and a score span | Shared button classes and a flexible row | A loop connects the monsters. |
| Chapter 7: Catch the Star | Game-area container with a star inside | A sized box and coordinates for the star | Timers and clicks change its position. |
| Chapters 8–12: canvas games | Drawing surface, instructions, status, sometimes Restart | Canvas dimensions, frame, and page layout | Drawing, movement, collisions, and game rules |
| Chapters 13–16: complete 2D projects | Canvas, toolbar, choices, movement buttons, status, error area | A reusable game page and shared stylesheet | Modules load assets and run the game. |
| Chapters 17–20: 3D projects | A stage container plus the same controls and messages | Space for a canvas created by the renderer | Three.js draws the world; Rapier adds physics where needed. |

Use this table as a map. Chapter 2 explains the HTML and CSS vocabulary for these structures before Chapter 3 begins teaching JavaScript variables.

::: {.callout-important collapse="true" title="Advanced Study: What is a local web server?" icon="false"}
Later games in this book will use several JavaScript files, data files, or 3D models. For those projects, we will sometimes run a **local web server**.

A local server is server software running on your own computer. It may give your browser an address such as:

```text
http://127.0.0.1:8000/
```

`127.0.0.1` is a special address that refers back to the same computer. Starting a local server for a project does **not** automatically publish that project to the Internet.

For now, you only need to recognize the idea. Later chapters will tell you when to use the local server and how to start it.
:::

## Challenges {.unnumbered}

# Build a Static Website with HTML and CSS {#sec-ch02}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[WEB 02 | Game Maker HQ]{.game-title}

[HTML]{.skill-chip} [CSS]{.skill-chip} [Forms]{.skill-chip} [Page structure]{.skill-chip}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .mission title="Your mission" icon="false"}

By the end of this chapter, you can:

- make an HTML page and connect a CSS file to it
- use headings, sections, lists, and classes to give a page structure
- use basic CSS rules, selectors, and declarations
- change font family, size, weight, and style to give a site its voice
- style a local image with size, borders, rounded corners, and a shadow
- add labeled text, menu, checkbox, and button input elements
- read the tags, attributes, and nested containers reused in later game pages
- explain the box model, flexible layouts, positioning, and canvas sizing
- use categorized HTML and CSS tables as a reference for the whole book

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="The big idea" icon="false"}

HTML says what belongs on a page. CSS says how it should look. Together they make a static website—the visual stage for the game. Chapter 3 adds JavaScript data; Chapter 4 connects that data to clicks and page updates.

:::

## Follow the same three-step development flow {#sec-ch02-development-flow}

**Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior.**

Before typing code, sketch the page. Ask what a player should see, how it should look, and what actions it should eventually support. For Game Maker HQ, the plan is:

| Step | Plan for this example | How to check it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Build the scene structure | Title, gem preview, mission list, and a player card with labeled controls | Open the plain HTML page and find every planned part. |
| 2. Style the scene | A centered card, readable fonts, a framed gem, and spaced controls | Link the stylesheet, refresh, and compare it with the plain page. |
| 3. Program game behavior | Later, read player choices and use them to set up a game | For now, write the desired action and expected result; no game logic is attached yet. |

HTML controls already let a person type or choose. In this flow, **behaviors** means the programmed game operations and actions you design, such as using those choices to start a game. Chapter 3 prepares their data; Chapter 4 begins connecting player actions to code.

For every small example below, identify its stage. An HTML-only fragment practices structure. A CSS-only fragment practices style on an existing structure. Neither fragment is a complete game action by itself. Save and check your work after each stage.

## Make the project folder

Create the folder from Chapter 1 and open it in your text editor:

```
my-game-site/
  index.html
  styles.css
  gem.svg
```

Keep the files in the same folder. The HTML file will use a `<link>` element to tell the browser where to find the CSS file. Copy [gem.svg](../games/assets/2d/gem.svg) from this textbook into your new folder so the page can show a local image.

## Step 1: Build the scene structure — build the page with HTML {#build-the-page-with-html}

Start with the **scene structure**: decide which parts belong on the page and place them in reading order. Save this complete example as `index.html`. HTML tags use angle brackets. Most tags have an opening tag and a matching closing tag; the content goes between them.

[COMPLETE EXAMPLE | `index.html`]{.code-label}

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Game Maker HQ</title>
  <!-- Step 2: Style the scene is supplied by the linked stylesheet. -->
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
</head>
<body>
  <!-- Step 1: Build the scene structure (page structure). -->
  <main class="card">
    <p class="eyebrow">MY STATIC WEBSITE</p>
    <h1>Game Maker HQ</h1>
    <p class="intro">Plan the next game you want to build.</p>

    <section class="game-preview">
      <img class="game-art" src="gem.svg"
           alt="A shiny purple gem for a game treasure.">
      <div>
        <h2>Gem Quest</h2>
        <p>Collect three gems, then open the portal.</p>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section>
      <h2>Today's missions</h2>
      <ul>
        <li>Sketch one game character.</li>
        <li>Choose a goal for the player.</li>
        <li>Invent a fair challenge.</li>
      </ul>
    </section>

    <section>
      <h2>Player card</h2>
      <form>
        <label for="player-name">Your game-maker name</label>
        <input id="player-name" name="player-name" type="text"
               placeholder="Type a nickname">

        <label for="game-type">Game type</label>
        <select id="game-type" name="game-type">
          <option>Adventure</option>
          <option>Puzzle</option>
          <option>Sports</option>
        </select>

        <label class="check-row" for="sound-on">
          <input id="sound-on" name="sound-on" type="checkbox">
          I want sound effects in my game.
        </label>

        <button type="button">My game will use this later</button>
      </form>
    </section>

    <!-- Step 3: Program game behavior — plan behaviors; game operations and actions come later. -->
    <p class="hint">This is a static site: the controls are ready, but JavaScript has not given them behavior yet.</p>
  </main>
</body>
</html>
```

Open `index.html` in a browser. If you edit it, save the file and refresh the browser tab. The page will have structure, but it will look plain until you add the CSS. A ready-to-run copy of these files is in `workspace/chapter2/`; open `plain.html` there to see the same page with its stylesheet link removed.

![The Game Maker HQ page in Chrome before its CSS file is linked. The headings, mission list, gem image, and player form appear in the browser's default style.](../figures/chapter_02/game-maker-hq-plain.png){#fig-ch02-plain-page fig-alt="A plain white browser page shows Game Maker HQ, a small gem, three missions, and a player form with default browser controls." width="100%"}

**Read the picture:** The content is already in a useful order: heading, game preview, missions, then player card. The gem loads because its `<img>` path points to a real local file. Without the stylesheet link, the browser supplies its default fonts, spacing, and control layout.

### Read the important HTML pieces {.unnumbered}

- `<head>` holds information *about* the page. The browser-tab title and the CSS link belong there.
- `<body>` holds the parts people see and use.
- `<main>` groups the main content. Its `class="card"` gives CSS a useful name for this group.
- `<h1>` and `<h2>` are headings. `<p>` is a paragraph. `<ul>` and `<li>` make a list.
- `<section>` groups a related part of the page.
- `<img>` puts the local `gem.svg` picture on the page. Its `alt` text describes the picture for people who cannot see it.

### Read a tag, an element, and an attribute {.unnumbered}

A **tag** marks the beginning or end of an HTML element. An **element** includes its opening tag, content, and closing tag. An **attribute** supplies extra information inside the opening tag.

```html
<button id="monster" class="monster" type="button">👾 Monster</button>
```

Here, `<button ...>` is the opening tag, `</button>` is the closing tag, and the words and emoji are the content. Together they form one button element. `id`, `class`, and `type` are attribute names; `"monster"`, `"monster"`, and `"button"` are their values. Write attributes in the opening tag, separated by spaces, and put their values in quotes.

Some elements are **void elements**: they have no content or closing tag. In our projects these include `<meta>`, `<link>`, `<img>`, `<input>`, and `<br>`. A `<canvas>` or `<script>` always needs its closing tag, even when it looks empty.

HTML comments look like `<!-- A note for the code reader -->`. The browser does not display them as page text. To display angle brackets as text, use `&lt;` for `<` and `&gt;` for `>`. For example, `<code>&lt;button&gt;</code>` displays the tag name instead of creating a button.

### Understand the document skeleton {.unnumbered}

Read the beginning of the complete example from top to bottom:

| Piece | Job | Why our games need it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `<!doctype html>` | Declares modern HTML; it is a declaration, not an element. | Helps the browser use its standard page-layout rules. |
| `<html lang="en">` | Contains the document and identifies English as its language. | Helps tools interpret the page, including spoken reading. |
| `<head>` | Contains information about the page and resource connections. | Holds the title, metadata, stylesheet, and sometimes an import map. |
| `<meta charset="utf-8">` | Chooses the text encoding. | Allows names, symbols, and emoji to be read correctly. |
| `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` | Sets the mobile layout viewport to the device width and an initial zoom of 1. | Makes our responsive CSS useful on small screens. |
| `<title>` | Names the browser tab. | Distinguishes an open game from other tabs; it does not create a visible heading. |
| `<link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">` | Loads a separate CSS file. | Lets several pages share a visual design. |
| `<body>` | Contains the page content and controls. | Holds the heading, game area, score, and buttons. |
| `<style>` | Holds CSS rules inside an HTML file, usually in the head. | Keeps later short game examples in one file. |
| `<script>` | Holds or loads JavaScript, depending on its attributes. | Provides the place for the game instructions starting in Chapter 3. |

The browser's reading order also matters. The early games put their ordinary `<script>` after the page elements it will use, just before `</body>`. Those elements exist when the script reaches them. In Chapter 3, you will fill that script with variables; you do not need to write those instructions yet.

### Nest elements to describe the page structure {.unnumbered}

**Nesting** means placing one element inside another. The outside element is the **parent**; the elements directly inside it are its **children**. Close the inner element before closing the outer one.

```html
<main>
  <section>
    <h2>Monster arena</h2>
    <div id="monsters">
      <button id="slime" class="monster" type="button">Slime</button>
      <button id="bat" class="monster" type="button">Bat</button>
    </div>
    <p>Score: <span id="score">0</span></p>
  </section>
</main>
```

`main` contains `section`. Inside the section, the heading, monster container, and score paragraph are siblings. The two buttons are children of the same `div`. Indentation makes these relationships easy to see; spaces alone do not create the relationships.

`<main>` identifies the main content, and `<section>` identifies a related topic, normally with a heading. `<div>` is a general container without a special topic meaning. It is useful for arranging a row of monster buttons or holding a 3D stage. `<span>` groups a small piece of content within a line. In the score paragraph, JavaScript will later update just the number inside the span.

Headings and paragraphs normally begin new blocks of content. A span normally stays in the surrounding line. CSS can change their layout, but choose the HTML element for its meaning first.

### HTML element reference for the whole book {#sec-ch02-html-reference}

The following tables cover the HTML used in the chapter code and the playable companion pages. Rows marked **extra workspace examples** describe the additional exploration pages shipped in `workspace/`, including `workspace/chapter1/`. They are optional practice, so their folder names do not define the current chapter sequence. The textbook's generated navigation and publishing theme are separate from the game code you write.

| Category | Elements | Meaning and example | Where you will meet them |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Document | `<html>`, `<head>`, `<body>` | Whole document, page information, visible content | Complete game pages throughout the book |
| Metadata and resources | `<meta>`, `<title>`, `<link>` | Encoding/viewport, tab title, stylesheet or tab icon | Chapters 2–4, 6, 8–12; Game Lab pages |
| Code containers | `<style>`, `<script>` | Embedded CSS; embedded or external JavaScript/data | Chapters 3–12; module projects in 13–20 |
| Main structure | `<main>`, `<section>` | Main content and a related section | Chapter 2, Monster Swarm, canvas games, Game Lab |
| Headings and text | `<h1>`, `<h2>`, `<p>` | Main heading, subsection heading, paragraph | Titles, instructions, scores, and messages |
| General groups | `<div>`, `<span>` | Container for a group; small part of a line | Chapter 6 monster row and score; Chapter 7 star; 3D stage |
| Lists | `<ul>`, `<ol>`, `<li>` | Bulleted list, numbered list, one list item | Chapter 2 missions; ordered missions in extra workspace examples |
| Navigation | `<a>` | Link to another page, a resource, or an ID such as `href="#missions"` | Game Lab menu and Back links |
| Pictures | `<img>` | Loads the picture named by `src`; `alt` supplies its text alternative | Chapter 2 gem; Chapter 4 image events |
| Drawing | `<canvas>` | Drawing surface with a coordinate space | Chapters 8–16; created by Three.js in 17–20 |
| Form group | `<form>` | Groups controls for collecting input | Chapter 2 player card |
| Control label | `<label>` | Gives a control an understandable name | Player card and Game Lab choices |
| Input and action | `<input>`, `<button>` | Text/checkbox/color and other controls; a pressable action | Chapter 2 onward; later game toolbars |
| Menu | `<select>`, `<option>` | Choice menu and one of its choices | Player card; Collision Playground shape choice |
| Meaning within text | `<strong>`, `<code>` | Important text; a code name or command shown as text | Game Lab cards and source-file hints |
| Extra page regions | `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<aside>`, `<footer>` | Introductory area, navigation area, related side note, closing information | Extra workspace examples |
| Extra form controls | `<textarea>`, `<fieldset>`, `<legend>` | Several lines of input, related-control group, group caption | Extra workspace player form |
| Extra table structure | `<table>`, `<thead>`, `<tbody>`, `<tr>`, `<th>`, `<td>` | Table, heading/body groups, row, header cell, data cell | Extra workspace element reference |
| Extra line break | `<br>` | A deliberate break inside text | Extra workspace example links; use CSS for spacing |

For a table, nest cells inside rows and rows inside the table's heading or body group. For example, `<thead><tr><th>Element</th><th>Job</th></tr></thead>` creates a heading row. `<th>` describes a heading cell; `<td>` describes an ordinary data cell. The summary tables in this chapter are written in Quarto's Markdown table syntax; Quarto creates the HTML table elements when it compiles the book.

### HTML attribute reference {#sec-ch02-attribute-reference}

An attribute's meaning depends on its element. `type="button"` on a button and `type="module"` on a script describe different things.

| Category | Attribute | What it means in our projects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Identity | `id` | A unique label in this document: `id="score"`. CSS can select it with `#score`; JavaScript will find it in Chapter 4. |
| Shared group | `class` | Reusable group names: `class="monster"`. Several elements can share a class, and one element can have several classes, such as `class="card primary"`. |
| Language | `lang` | The content language, such as `lang="en"` on `html`. |
| Encoding | `charset` | The encoding on `meta`, here `utf-8`. |
| Named metadata | `name`, `content` | On `meta`, identify a setting and its value, such as the viewport. |
| Resource relationship | `rel` | On `link`, explains the resource's purpose: `stylesheet` for CSS, `icon` for the tab picture. |
| Link destination | `href` | Where an `a` or `link` points. `#missions` points to an ID on this page. |
| Resource source | `src` | Where an `img` or external `script` loads its resource. |
| Picture alternative | `alt` | Describes the image's meaning; a purely decorative image can use `alt=""`. |
| Dimensions | `width`, `height` | On images, dimension hints; on canvas, the drawing-space dimensions. Use numbers such as `width="500"`, without `px`. |
| Label connection | `for` | On `label`, matches the control's `id`, such as `for="player-name"`. |
| Control name | `name` | Names form data; radio buttons sharing a name form a choice group. This does not replace an ID. |
| Control kind | `type` | On `input`: `text`, `checkbox`, `color`, and other kinds. On `button`: `button` prevents ordinary form submission. |
| Starting input | `value`, `placeholder` | `value` sets initial input content or an option's data value. `placeholder` is a temporary hint in an empty text input, not a label. |
| Starting state | `checked` | Starts a checkbox or radio button checked. It is a Boolean attribute: its presence means true; `checked="false"` still checks it. |
| Visibility | `hidden` | Initially hides the Game Lab error box. For the plain `hidden` used here, omit it to show the box; `hidden="false"` still hides it. |
| Script/data kind | `type` | On `script`: `module` enables JavaScript modules; `importmap` identifies mapping data. On an icon `link`, `image/svg+xml` identifies the image format. |
| Accessible name | `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby` | Supply a name directly, or refer to the ID of visible text that names the region/control. Used for game surfaces, controls, and extra workspace sections. |
| Live message | `role`, `aria-live` | `role="status"` identifies a status message. `aria-live="polite"` asks assistive technology to announce changes at a suitable pause. |
| Decorative content | `aria-hidden` | `aria-hidden="true"` keeps decorative content out of the accessibility tree. It does not visually hide it. |
| Custom game data | `data-key`, `data-move` | Store our own labels: a movement key in the Game Lab or a move in extra choice-game examples. They do not create behavior on their own. |
| Keyboard focus | `tabindex` | `tabindex="0"` lets a canvas join the normal Tab-key order. The Game Lab input helper sets the matching JavaScript property `tabIndex`. |
| File download | `download` | Suggests a filename when an anchor downloads a resource. The Asset Workshop sets this through JavaScript when exporting a model. |
| Extra input limits | `min`, `max` | Bounds for number/range controls in extra workspace examples. |
| Extra text area | `rows` | Visible text-line count for a textarea, such as `rows="3"`. |
| Extra autofill | `autocomplete` | Gives an autofill hint, such as `autocomplete="nickname"`. |

IDs and classes are names you choose. `monster`, `card`, and `game-art` are not built-in HTML commands. Each ID must be unique in its page, while a class is useful precisely because several elements can share it. Match spelling and capitalization when referring to those names.

A path is relative to the HTML page unless another base is specified. `gem.svg` means a file beside the page, `assets/gem.svg` means inside a child folder, and `../assets/gem.svg` goes up one folder first. Moving a page without its related files can break its links. The Game Lab uses paths such as `../shared/lab.css` because its games share one stylesheet.

::: {.callout-note title="Attributes, CSS properties, and DOM properties are different" icon="false"}
In `<canvas width="500">`, `width` is an **HTML attribute**. In `canvas { width: 100%; }`, `width` is a **CSS property**. Later, `canvas.width` is a **JavaScript property** on the browser's canvas element. These affect related parts of the page, but they use different syntax and can describe different sizes.

Likewise, `checked` in HTML is a checkbox's starting state; JavaScript's `.checked` reads its current state. `.value` reads current input, `.textContent` changes text, and `.style.left` changes a CSS position. Chapter 4 teaches the DOM; Chapter 7 uses style properties for movement. You only need to recognize the distinction now.
:::

## CSS basics: rules change how HTML looks

CSS is a list of rules. A rule starts with a **selector**—the HTML element or class that you want to style. Inside the braces, each **declaration** has a property, a colon, a value, and a semicolon.

```css
selector {
  property: value;
}
```

Read this rule aloud as: “For every element with the class `game-art`, make the border rounded.”

```css
.game-art {
  border-radius: 24px;
}
```

The dot is important. `.game-art` means “find `class="game-art"` in the HTML.” An element selector has no dot: `h1` styles every level-one heading and `img` styles every image. You can write more than one declaration inside the same braces.

| Selector | What it selects | Example use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `body` | the whole visible page | choose a default font and text color |
| `h1` | every main heading | make the title large and bold |
| `.intro` | elements with `class="intro"` | make the introduction italic |
| `.game-art` | the gem image with that class | set the image's frame and size |

## Step 2: Style the scene — make the scene readable {#style-fonts-and-images-with-css}

The scene is built. Now **style the scene** with size, spacing, colors, fonts, and layout. Save this in a second file named `styles.css`. Keep the same HTML so you can see exactly what styling changes.

[COMPLETE EXAMPLE | `styles.css`]{.code-label}

```css
/* Step 2: Style the scene; this file adds no game actions. */
:root {
  --ink: #17243b;
  --paper: #f7f4ff;
  --purple: #6d3df5;
  --yellow: #ffe48a;
}

* {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

body {
  margin: 0;
  min-height: 100vh;
  display: grid;
  place-items: center;
  background: linear-gradient(135deg, #c9efff, var(--paper));
  color: var(--ink);
  font-family: "Trebuchet MS", Verdana, sans-serif;
  font-size: 1rem;
  line-height: 1.6;
}

.card {
  width: min(92%, 620px);
  margin: 32px;
  padding: 32px;
  border: 4px solid var(--ink);
  border-radius: 24px;
  background: white;
  box-shadow: 10px 10px 0 var(--yellow);
}

.eyebrow {
  margin: 0;
  color: var(--purple);
  font-family: Verdana, sans-serif;
  font-size: 0.8rem;
  font-weight: 700;
  letter-spacing: 0.08em;
}

h1 {
  margin: 8px 0;
  color: var(--purple);
  font-family: Georgia, "Times New Roman", serif;
  font-size: clamp(2.2rem, 7vw, 3.5rem);
  font-weight: 800;
  line-height: 1.1;
}

.intro {
  color: #4c3f74;
  font-size: 1.15rem;
  font-style: italic;
}

.hint {
  font-size: 0.9rem;
}

.game-preview {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 22px;
  margin-top: 28px;
  padding: 18px;
  border: 2px solid #b7aee5;
  border-radius: 20px;
  background: #f2edff;
}

.game-preview h2 {
  margin: 0;
  font-family: Georgia, "Times New Roman", serif;
}

.game-preview p {
  margin: 4px 0 0;
}

.game-art {
  width: 140px;
  height: 140px;
  padding: 14px;
  border: 4px solid var(--purple);
  border-radius: 24px;
  background: white;
  box-shadow: 7px 7px 0 var(--yellow);
  object-fit: contain;
}

section {
  margin-top: 28px;
  padding-top: 8px;
  border-top: 2px dashed #b7aee5;
}

form {
  display: grid;
  gap: 10px;
}

input,
select,
button {
  min-height: 44px;
  padding: 10px 12px;
  border: 2px solid var(--ink);
  border-radius: 10px;
  font: inherit;
}

.check-row {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 8px;
}

.check-row input {
  min-height: auto;
}

button {
  margin-top: 8px;
  background: var(--purple);
  color: white;
  cursor: pointer;
  font-weight: 800;
}

button:hover {
  background: #4d24c8;
}

input:focus-visible,
select:focus-visible,
button:focus-visible {
  outline: 4px solid var(--yellow);
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

@media (max-width: 520px) {
  .game-preview {
    align-items: flex-start;
    flex-direction: column;
  }
}
```

Save `styles.css` beside `index.html`, then refresh the page. Compare this browser result with the plain version above. The HTML content is the same; the linked CSS file changes its appearance.

![The Game Maker HQ page in Chrome after the linked CSS file is loaded. A centered white card contains a large purple title, framed gem preview, spaced missions, and stacked form controls.](../figures/chapter_02/game-maker-hq-styled.png){#fig-ch02-styled-page fig-alt="A styled Game Maker HQ page has a pale blue background, white card, purple title, framed gem, mission list, and full-width player form controls." width="100%"}

**Read the picture:** `.card` makes the white panel, `.game-preview` arranges the gem and its text, and `.game-art` adds the gem's rounded frame and shadow. The `form` rule stacks the labeled controls. Try changing one CSS value, saving, and refreshing to see which part of this picture changes.

### Give the site a readable voice {.unnumbered}

```css
body {
  font-family: "Trebuchet MS", Verdana, sans-serif;
}

h1 {
  font-family: Georgia, "Times New Roman", serif;
  font-size: clamp(2.2rem, 7vw, 3.5rem);
  font-weight: 800;
}

.intro {
  font-style: italic;
}
```

`font-family` chooses the lettering style. The comma-separated names are a **font stack**: the browser tries the first font and then tries the next one if needed. The last name, such as `sans-serif` or `serif`, is a broad backup family, so the page still has a sensible look on another computer.

`font-size` changes how large the letters appear. `font-weight` changes how thick they look: `400` is similar to normal text, while `700` is similar to bold. `font-style: italic` adds a slant for emphasis. Use the right HTML tag first—an `<h1>` should still be the main heading even if you later change its size with CSS.

### Frame an image with CSS {.unnumbered}

```css
.game-art {
  width: 140px;
  padding: 14px;
  border: 4px solid var(--purple);
  border-radius: 24px;
  box-shadow: 7px 7px 0 var(--yellow);
}
```

`width` keeps the image at a friendly size. `padding` adds breathing room inside its frame. `border` draws the edge, `border-radius` rounds the corners, and `box-shadow` makes the gem look as if it is resting above the card. Try changing `border-radius` to `50%`; the square frame becomes a circle.

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="Practice CSS one property at a time" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL DEEPER DIVE]{.study-badge}

Change one value, save the CSS file, and refresh the browser. That small experiment tells you exactly which property made the difference. Helpful next references are the [W3Schools CSS tutorial](https://www.w3schools.com/css/), [CSS Fonts](https://www.w3schools.com/css/css_font.asp), and [CSS Styling Images](https://www.w3schools.com/css/css3_images.asp).
