## Understand the CSS that our games reuse {#sec-ch02-css-reference}

The complete stylesheet above already uses layout, size limits, custom colors, and responsive rules. Read these explanations with the page open. Change one value at a time so that each rule has a visible meaning.

### Selectors find the right elements {.unnumbered}

A selector chooses **which elements** get a rule; the declarations choose **what changes**. An HTML class name has no dot, but a CSS class selector does. An HTML ID has no hash mark, but a CSS ID selector does.

| Selector category | Example from our pages | Read it as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Element | `canvas` | Every canvas element |
| Class | `.monster` | Every element with the class `monster` |
| ID | `#star` | The element with `id="star"` |
| Universal | `*` | Every element; used for consistent box sizing |
| Root | `:root` | The document's root element; a useful place for shared color variables |
| Selector list | `input, select, button` | Apply the same declarations to each listed kind |
| Descendant | `.game-preview h2` | An `h2` anywhere inside an element with class `game-preview` |
| Combined element/class | `button.primary` | A button that also has class `primary` |
| Attribute | `button[data-key]` | A button carrying a `data-key` attribute |
| Attribute value | `input[type="color"]` | An input whose type is `color`, in the extra workspace form |
| Hover state | `button:hover` | A button while a pointer is over it |
| Visible focus state | `button:focus-visible` | A focused button when the browser determines a focus indicator should be shown, commonly during keyboard use |

A space in `.game-preview h2` means “inside”; a comma in `input, select, button` means “any of these.” `button.primary` has no space because both conditions describe the same element. Later rules such as `#stage canvas` style the renderer's canvas inside the 3D stage.

### Understand inheritance and competing rules {.unnumbered}

Text properties such as `color` and `font-family` often pass from a parent to its children. This is **inheritance**. The `body` rule sets a default font; the `h1` rule chooses a different one. `font: inherit` asks form controls to use their parent's font settings. Borders, padding, and margins do not normally inherit.

Several rules can match the same element. In our ordinary stylesheets, a more specific selector wins when competing declarations have the same importance and origin. For example, `#star` is more specific than `span`, and `.game-preview h2` is more specific than `h2`. If specificity is tied, the later declaration wins. These selection rules are part of the **cascade**.

```css
button { background: purple; }
button { background: teal; }
```

The second rule wins here. This does not mean that the last rule always wins: selector specificity still matters. CSS comments use `/* A note for the code reader */`; the browser ignores the comment.

### Every element has a box {.unnumbered}

Imagine four layers: the content, its inner padding, its border, and the margin outside that border. This is the **box model**.

```text
margin: space outside the box
  border: the box's edge
    padding: space inside the edge
      content: text, picture, or drawing surface
```

With `box-sizing: border-box`, the CSS width includes the content, padding, and border. A box with `width: 140px`, `padding: 14px`, and `border: 4px solid purple` still has a total border-box width of 140 pixels; its content gets the space left inside. Margin is outside that width. Without `border-box`, those padding and border widths would be added to the content width.

Read spacing shorthand clockwise: `margin: 10px 20px 30px 40px` sets top, right, bottom, and left. Two values such as `padding: 10px 12px` mean vertical then horizontal. Three values such as `margin: 4px 0 0` mean top, horizontal, then bottom. One value applies to all four sides. A side-specific property such as `margin-top` changes just that side.

`margin: 40px auto` gives 40 pixels above and below and automatic left/right margins. For an ordinary block with a limited width, those automatic margins center it horizontally. `min-height: 1.5em` reserves message space even when the message is short, so the page does not jump as much when the text changes.

### Read sizes, colors, and functions {.unnumbered}

CSS values carry units. Write `140px`, not just `140`, for a pixel length. Zero can be written without a unit, and properties such as `font-weight` or a relative `line-height` use unitless numbers.

| Value kind | Examples in our projects | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CSS pixels | `140px`, `24px` | A CSS layout unit, useful for frames and game-area sizes; not necessarily one physical display pixel |
| Percentage | `92%`, `100%`, `50%` | Relative to a relevant size; width usually uses the containing box, while `border-radius: 50%` uses the element's own dimensions |
| Root-font size | `1rem`, `2.2rem` | Relative to the root element's font size |
| Local-font size | `1.5em`, `0.08em` | In our message height and letter spacing, relative to that element's font size |
| Viewport size | `7vw`, `100vh` | One `vw` is 1% of viewport width; one `vh` is 1% of viewport height |
| Flexible grid share | `1fr` | One share of the space available to grid tracks |
| Named/hex color | `white`, `#6d3df5`, `#333` | A color name or hexadecimal red/green/blue values; short hex repeats each digit |
| Transparent color | `rgba(255, 255, 255, .92)`, `#2237540b`, `transparent` | A color with opacity, an eight-digit hex color with alpha, or no visible color |
| Custom property | `--purple: #6d3df5` and `var(--purple)` | Define a reusable value and retrieve it |
| Smaller value | `min(92%, 620px)` | Use the smaller result: the card fits its container and never grows past 620 pixels |
| Bounded value | `clamp(2.2rem, 7vw, 3.5rem)` | Use the middle value while keeping it between a minimum and a maximum |
| Calculation | `calc(100% - 40px)` | Calculate a size; used by the extra workspace pages |
| Grid functions | `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(230px, 1fr))` | Repeat as many tracks as fit, with a 230-pixel minimum and room to share extra width |
| Gradient | `linear-gradient(135deg, #c9efff, var(--paper))` | Blend colors along a direction; `deg` measures the angle |
| Extra radial gradient | `radial-gradient(circle, white, transparent)` | Blend colors outward from a center; used in the extra workspace background |
| Automatic/default value | `auto`, `inherit`, `none` | Let sizing be automatic, reuse a parent's value, or disable a feature, depending on the property |

A **custom property** starts with `--`. In this chapter, `:root` defines `--ink`, `--paper`, `--purple`, and `--yellow`. The extra workspace palette also uses `--muted`, `--purple-dark`, `--aqua`, and `--line`. These are our chosen names. Change one shared color and every rule using that `var(...)` value can change with it.

### Arrange a page with Grid and Flexbox {.unnumbered}

Normal page flow places headings and paragraphs in document order. `display: block` gives an element a block box; the canvas games use it to put the drawing surface on its own line. `display: inline-block` gives a badge a box while letting it sit in a line of text.

`display: grid` arranges children in rows and columns. In our Chapter 2 `body`, `place-items: center` centers the card within its grid area, and `min-height: 100vh` gives the page at least a viewport of height. The `form` uses a one-column grid with `gap: 10px` to separate controls. The Game Lab's `.cards` uses `grid-template-columns` to make several card columns when space allows.

`display: flex` arranges children along a main direction. The game preview places the gem and its text side by side. `gap` separates the children. `align-items: center` lines them up across the main direction; `justify-content: center` centers them along the main direction. Monster Swarm uses this to center its buttons. `flex-wrap: wrap` lets a long row continue onto another line.

```css
#monsters {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: center;
  align-items: center;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  gap: 12px;
}
```

The default flex direction is a row. `flex-direction: column` changes it to a column. In this chapter's small-screen rule, `align-items: flex-start` places the column's children at its start edge.

### Make the layout respond to the screen {.unnumbered}

An **at-rule** begins with `@`. Our `@media` rule applies its nested CSS only when a condition matches:

```css
@media (max-width: 520px) {
  .game-preview {
    align-items: flex-start;
    flex-direction: column;
  }
}
```

When the viewport is at most 520 CSS pixels wide, the preview stacks vertically. The Game Lab uses a 600-pixel breakpoint; the extra workspace pages use 760 pixels. A **breakpoint** is a chosen layout threshold, not a special type of device. Resize the browser to see the rule start and stop applying. Flexible widths, size limits, and media queries work together; adding viewport metadata alone does not make a fixed-width game fit every screen.

### Position a game object inside its play area {.unnumbered}

Chapter 7 uses an ordinary HTML star inside a game container. You can prepare its starting position with CSS before adding a timer:

```html
<div id="game"><span id="star">⭐</span></div>
```

```css
#game {
  position: relative;
  width: 340px;
  height: 240px;
  border: 2px solid #333;
}

#star {
  position: absolute;
  left: 120px;
  top: 80px;
  font-size: 36px;
  cursor: pointer;
}
```

`position: relative` keeps the game box in normal flow and makes it the reference box for the absolutely positioned star. `position: absolute` takes the star out of normal flow. `left` and `top` place it relative to that reference box: 120 pixels from the left, 80 from the top. Increasing `left` moves right; increasing `top` moves down.

Keep the star's width and height in mind when choosing a position. An object whose left edge is inside the play area can still stick out at the right. Chapter 7 changes these same CSS properties through JavaScript; the positioning system itself is already in place.

### Prepare a canvas and a 3D stage {.unnumbered}

A canvas is one HTML element, even when JavaScript draws many balls, bricks, or characters inside it. Those drawings are not separate HTML buttons or spans.

```html
<canvas id="game" width="500" height="300"
        aria-label="Game drawing area">This game needs Canvas support.</canvas>
```

```css
canvas {
  display: block;
  width: 100%;
  max-width: 500px;
  height: auto;
  border: 2px solid #17243b;
  background: #f0f7ff;
}
```

HTML `width="500" height="300"` sets the drawing coordinate space. CSS sizes its display box. In this example, a narrower container can show a smaller version of the same drawing without changing those coordinates. `height: auto` keeps the canvas's proportions. Arbitrarily changing both displayed dimensions can stretch the picture. Chapter 13 explains how pointer coordinates must be scaled when drawing size and display size differ. See the [MDN canvas reference](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/canvas).

The canvas stays blank until JavaScript draws. Fallback text does not describe every drawn object, and an accessible label does not make all canvas gameplay accessible. Keep useful instructions and status information in ordinary HTML alongside the game.

For Chapters 17–20, the HTML starts with a host such as `<div id="stage"></div>`. Three.js creates a canvas and attaches it inside that div. The Game Lab gives `#stage` a height, rounded corners, and `overflow: hidden` so drawing outside its box is clipped. `#stage canvas` styles the child canvas. CSS controls the page frame; JavaScript and the renderer control the 3D world.

### CSS property summary: text and appearance {.unnumbered}

These tables include the properties in the chapter examples, the shared Game Lab stylesheet, and the supplied workspace practice pages. A comma-separated group lists related properties, not one property with a long name. The optional Game Lab rows are a reference to return to when those projects begin.

| Category | Property | Job and example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lettering | `font-family` | Choose a font stack: `system-ui, sans-serif`. |
| Letter size | `font-size` | Set text size: `1.1rem` or `36px`. |
| Emphasis | `font-weight`, `font-style` | Set thickness (`700`, `bold`) and slant (`italic`). |
| Font shorthand | `font` | Set several font settings together; `font: inherit` copies the parent's font settings. |
| Text spacing | `line-height`, `letter-spacing` | Separate lines (`1.6`) and letters (`0.08em`). |
| Text alignment | `text-align` | Align text inside a box: `center` in Monster Swarm, `left` in tables. |
| Links | `text-decoration` | Control decoration such as underlining; Game Lab card links use `none`. |
| Extra link details | `text-decoration-thickness`, `text-underline-offset` | Set underline thickness and distance from letters in workspace navigation. |
| Foreground | `color` | Choose text color: `#17243b`. |
| Surface | `background` | Set a surface color or image/gradient; canvas CSS colors the surface, not individual drawn objects. |
| Frame | `border` | Width, line style, color: `2px solid #17243b`; `dashed` makes a dashed line. |
| Frame sides | `border-top`, `border-bottom`, `border-left`, `border-color` | Change one border side or its color; section separators use these. |
| Corners | `border-radius` | Round the frame: `24px`; `50%` makes a square frame circular. |
| Shadow | `box-shadow` | Offset, blur, optional spread, color; `7px 7px 0 var(--yellow)` has no blur. |
| Image fit | `object-fit` | `contain` keeps the whole picture visible within its content box without stretching it. |
| Focus indicator | `outline`, `outline-offset` | Draw a focus ring and separate it from the border; unlike a border, the outline does not occupy layout space. |
| Pointer cue | `cursor` | `pointer` suggests a clickable target; it does not add a click handler. |

### CSS property summary: size, space, and layout {.unnumbered}

| Category | Property | Job and example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Box size | `width`, `height` | Set dimensions: the gem frame is 140 by 140 pixels; the star arena is 340 by 240. |
| Size limits | `min-width`, `max-width`, `min-height`, `max-height` | Set bounds; the Game Lab reserves a minimum stage height and limits canvas height. |
| Width accounting | `box-sizing` | `border-box` includes border and padding in the stated CSS size. |
| Outer spacing | `margin`, `margin-top`, `margin-bottom` | Separate a box from other content or center it with horizontal `auto` margins. |
| Inner spacing | `padding`, `padding-top`, `padding-bottom`, `padding-left` | Separate content from its border; workspace lists add left padding. |
| Layout mode | `display` | Choose `block`, `inline-block`, `grid`, or `flex` for the jobs explained above. |
| Between children | `gap` | Space between grid/flex items: `12px` between monsters. |
| Flex direction | `flex-direction` | Arrange children in a `row` or `column`. |
| Flex wrapping | `flex-wrap` | `wrap` allows another line when a row becomes too long. |
| Alignment | `align-items`, `justify-content`, `place-items` | Align across a flex row, distribute along it, or align grid items on both axes. |
| Grid tracks | `grid-template-columns` | Describe columns; `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(230px, 1fr))` makes flexible Game Lab cards. |
| Positioned objects | `position`, `left`, `top` | Choose the positioning method and offsets; Catch the Star uses `relative` and `absolute`. |
| Overflow | `overflow` | `hidden` clips content outside the box; used for the 3D stage. |

### Optional CSS reference: Game Lab and extra workspace details {.unnumbered}

| Category | Property or construct | What it does in the supplied examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shared palette | Custom properties `--ink`, `--paper`, `--purple`, `--yellow`, `--muted`, `--purple-dark`, `--aqua`, `--line`; `var()` | Store and reuse named theme values. The names are chosen by us. |
| Conditional layout | `@media (max-width: ...)` | Apply nested rules below a viewport-width threshold. This is an at-rule, not a property. |
| Browser control theme | `color-scheme` | `light` asks browser-rendered controls to use a light scheme; it does not set every page color. |
| Hover appearance | `filter` | `brightness(.96)` slightly darkens the Game Lab's hovered buttons. |
| Touch behavior | `touch-action` | `none` reserves touch gestures on game surfaces/buttons for the interaction code instead of browser panning/zooming there. |
| Text selection | `user-select` | `none` prevents selecting movement-button text during play. |
| Error formatting | `white-space` | `pre-wrap` preserves spaces and line breaks while allowing long error text to wrap. |
| Screen-reader utility | `clip` | The supplied `.sr-only` rule uses `rect(0,0,0,0)` with absolute positioning, a tiny box, and hidden overflow to conceal content visually. This older property is deprecated; recognize it in the existing stylesheet rather than choose it for a new design. |
| Extra table borders | `border-collapse` | `collapse` merges neighboring table-cell borders. |
| Extra control color | `accent-color` | Colors supported native control accents, such as the range slider. |
| Extra text-area resizing | `resize` | `vertical` lets the player change a textarea's height. |
| Extra hover motion | `transform` | `translateY(-3px)` shifts a link upward visually without rearranging normal flow. |
| Extra gradual change | `transition` | `transform .15s ease, box-shadow .15s ease` smooths changes over 0.15 seconds. `s` means seconds and `ease` controls the timing curve. |

The `.sr-only` class is a supplied utility rule, not a requirement to conceal your instructions. It differs from HTML `hidden`, which also removes ordinary hidden content from assistive reading. For the legacy property's status, see [MDN: clip](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Properties/clip).

CSS styles HTML boxes. Later code such as `ctx.fillStyle`, `ctx.strokeStyle`, and `ctx.font` controls canvas drawing; Three.js material colors control 3D surfaces. Those are JavaScript drawing settings, not additional CSS properties. Return to the appropriate drawing chapter when changing a ball, sprite, or model.

## Step 3: Program game behavior — plan game operations and actions {#prepare-the-inputs-for-javascript}

Start the **behavior** step with a rule in words: “When the player presses the button, read the nickname and game choices, then use them to prepare a game.” This is a plan, not an instruction to add click-handling code in Chapter 2.

The text box, menu, checkbox, and button are all **input elements**: parts of a page a person can use. Their labels make the controls easier to understand and help assistive technology describe them.

Look closely at this pair:

```html
<label for="player-name">Your game-maker name</label>
<input id="player-name" name="player-name" type="text">
```

The label's `for="player-name"` matches the input's `id="player-name"`. That connection means clicking the words “Your game-maker name” focuses the correct text box. The `id` will also let JavaScript find this exact element later.

The button uses `type="button"`. It looks and feels like a button, but it has no task yet. It will not submit the form or save the choices. JavaScript needs to listen for a click, read the inputs, and decide what to do.

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="Static does not mean unfinished" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL DEEPER DIVE]{.study-badge}

Static pages are excellent for information, art portfolios, instructions, and game-planning pages. HTML gives them a sensible order; CSS makes them readable and expressive. HTML controls and CSS states already provide some interaction. JavaScript adds programmed responses, calculations, game memory, data loading, and changes such as score updates.

The browser may remember what you typed for a moment, but this example has no code to save a player name. Refreshing or reopening the page can clear it. Code that remembers choices comes later.

:::

### Choose a control for the player's task {.unnumbered}

Controls have built-in browser behavior even before you write game logic. A text box accepts typing, a checkbox toggles, and a select menu changes its selected option. Your Chapter 2 button has no application-specific action yet. JavaScript will supply that action later.

| Control kind | HTML pattern | Purpose in our examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Text | `<input type="text">` | Player nickname |
| Checkbox | `<input type="checkbox">` | Sound or wall-blocking on/off |
| Color | `<input type="color" value="#20b7a5">` | Robot body color in the Chapter 18 Asset Workshop |
| Choice menu | `<select><option value="box">Rectangle</option></select>` | Game type or Collision Playground shape; the data value can differ from visible text |
| Action | `<button type="button">Restart</button>` | A game action connected by JavaScript |
| Extra numeric input | `<input type="number" min="1" max="10">` | A numeric choice in the extra workspace examples |
| Extra slider | `<input type="range" min="1" max="10" value="7">` | A bounded setting such as hero speed |
| Extra single choice | `<input type="radio" name="power">` | One choice from the radios sharing `name="power"` |
| Extra email/date | `<input type="email">`, `<input type="date">` | Browser controls for these kinds of input in the extra player form |
| Extra longer text | `<textarea rows="3">My game idea</textarea>` | Several lines; the initial text goes between its tags |

You can connect a label with `for` and a matching ID, as in the player card. You can also place the input inside its label: `<label><input type="checkbox"> Sound</label>`. The Game Lab uses this second pattern for compact checkboxes. A `fieldset` with a `legend` can give related controls, such as a group of radio choices, one shared description.

### Recognize the three ways scripts appear {.unnumbered}

You do not need to write a module or an import map in this chapter. Learn what their HTML wrappers mean so the later projects have a familiar page structure.

| Script form | HTML | Meaning and later use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inline ordinary script | `<script>` followed by code and `</script>` | Code stored in the page; Chapters 3–12 usually put it after the visible elements. |
| External module | `<script type="module" src="game.js"></script>` | Load a JavaScript file that can import/export other modules; introduced in Chapter 12 and used in the Game Lab. |
| Import map | `<script type="importmap">` followed by JSON and `</script>` | Data mapping module names to resource addresses; Chapter 17 uses it for Three.js. Put it before the module that needs the map. |

Module scripts are deferred until the HTML has been parsed, and their dependencies must load before they can run. Module-based game projects use the local server introduced in Chapter 1 and set up in the Game Lab guide. An import map contains data, not game instructions; Chapter 17 explains its actual entries. See [MDN: script](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script).

## Rehearse the page that Chapter 3 will use {#sec-ch02-monster-page}

Use **Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior** again. Before working with variables, make a small **static Monster Clicker page**. This connects the Game Maker HQ skills to the next chapter. Create a separate `monster-page/` folder with `index.html` and `styles.css`; keep your HQ project too.

**Step 1 — Build the scene structure:** make the title, monster button, message, and score. Their IDs identify the parts that later actions will use.

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Monster Clicker</title>
  <!-- Step 2: Style the scene with styles.css. -->
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
</head>
<body>
  <!-- Step 1: Build the scene structure (page structure). -->
  <main class="card">
    <h1>Monster Clicker</h1>
    <p>Meet the monster. Its click action comes in Chapter 4.</p>
    <button id="monster" class="monster" type="button">👾 Monster</button>
    <p id="message">The monster is waiting...</p>
    <p id="score">Score: 0</p>
  </main>
  <script>
    // Step 3: Program game behavior: prepare data in Chapter 3 and click actions in Chapter 4.
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

The empty script contains only a JavaScript comment beginning with `//`. It creates a place for later instructions without adding game behavior.

**Step 2 — Style the scene:** save this small stylesheet beside the page. It makes the existing scene readable without changing its game rules:

```css
/* Step 2: Style the scene. */
* { box-sizing: border-box; }
body {
  margin: 0;
  min-height: 100vh;
  display: grid;
  place-items: center;
  background: #eef7ff;
  color: #17243b;
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
}
.card {
  width: min(92%, 620px);
  padding: 24px;
  border: 3px solid #17243b;
  border-radius: 20px;
  background: white;
}
#monster {
  padding: 18px;
  border: 2px solid #17243b;
  border-radius: 14px;
  background: #e7dcff;
  font: inherit;
  cursor: pointer;
}
#monster:focus-visible {
  outline: 4px solid #ffe48a;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}
#message { min-height: 1.5em; }
```

Open the page, then locate the heading, button, message, and score in the source. Explain how `#monster` in CSS refers to `id="monster"` in HTML. Press Tab to focus the button and observe the focus ring. Clicking the monster does not change the score yet: appearance and game rules are separate jobs.

**Step 3 — Program game behavior:** write the rule “When the monster is hit, increase the score and show a message.” The page does not implement that rule yet. Chapter 3 keeps the scene and style and fills the script with the data needed by the rule. A runnable copy of this static rehearsal is in `workspace/chapter2/monster-page/`. Chapter 4 adds the DOM and event code. The familiar HTML is the stage for those new JavaScript ideas.

### Apply the flow to every example {.unnumbered}

Use this table when practicing the smaller examples as well as the complete page. Each row begins with something that exists in the scene, then a visual choice, then a possible game action.

| Example | 1. Build the scene structure | 2. Style the scene | 3. Program game behavior: planned or taught later |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Game Maker HQ | Preview, missions, labeled player controls | Card, fonts, gem frame, form layout | Read choices and prepare a game; plan only here. |
| Nested monster group | Container, buttons, score span | Shared button class and flexible row | Hit a monster and update the score; Chapters 4–6. |
| Gem picture | An image with a source and text alternative | Size, padding, border, shadow | Collect the gem on an action; Chapter 4's image example. |
| Static star arena | A game div containing a star span | Relative parent; absolute star with left/top | Move the star on clicks and timer ticks; Chapter 7. |
| Canvas preview | A drawing surface with dimensions and instructions | Border, background, responsive display size | Draw and move game objects; Chapters 8 onward. |
| 3D stage preview | A stage host, controls, and status area | Stage height and clipped drawing area | Load and render a 3D world; Chapters 17–20. |
| Monster Clicker rehearsal | Title, monster, message, score | Card and monster button styling | Prepare memory in Chapter 3; connect the hit action in Chapter 4. |

The font, image-frame, selector, and layout snippets each practice **Step 2: Style the scene** on one of these existing structures. The HTML control and container snippets practice **Step 1: Build the scene structure**. For an extra workspace page, trace the same three stages before changing it.

### Page-structure summary for later projects {.unnumbered}

| Project stage | Visible page structure | CSS to recognize | New work left for JavaScript |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Chapters 3–5 | Heading → monster/actions → message and score → script | Font, color, frame, spacing, ID selectors | Variables, clicks, score updates, decisions |
| Chapter 6 | Main card → score span → container of monster buttons → Power Hit/message | Shared `.monster` class, Flexbox, wrapping, gap, reserved message height | Loop over monsters |
| Chapter 7 | Heading/score → game div containing the star | Sized container, relative/absolute positioning, left/top | Random positions and timers |
| Chapters 8–12 | Heading/instructions → canvas → status and optional Restart | Canvas frame, block layout, centered card | Drawing and game rules |
| Chapters 13–16 | Main → panel → toolbar/choices → status → canvas → movement controls → error area | Shared `lab.css`, flexible toolbar, responsive canvas, focus and touch rules | Modules, loading, real-time input and simulation |
| Chapters 17–20 | Same game-page pattern, with a stage div containing a renderer-created canvas | Stage height, child selector, overflow, responsive size limits | Imports, renderer, models, and physics where needed |

For each task, first locate the existing scene parts, check their style, and name the expected operation. The notes identify what changes; keep the other stages when they already meet the goal.

# Teach the Game to Remember {#sec-ch03}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[GAME 03 | Monster Clicker Starter]{.game-title}

[Variables]{.skill-chip} [Data Types]{.skill-chip} [Arrays]{.skill-chip} [Objects]{.skill-chip}

:::

## Overview

Keep using our development flow:

**Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior.**

First use HTML to build what the player sees and uses. Next use CSS to make that scene readable. Then use JavaScript to implement the game's operations and actions. This chapter begins the behavior stage by giving those actions **data and memory**; Chapter 4 connects them to clicks.

Before a game can react to a player, it needs something very important: **memory**.

A game may need to remember:

- the player's score;
- the player's name;
- the number of lives left;
- whether the game has started;
- which treasures have been collected;
- information about the player or a monster.

JavaScript stores these values in **variables**.

In this chapter, you will build the starting version of a **Monster Clicker** project. The monster will appear on the page, and JavaScript will create the data the game needs. The monster will not react to a click yet. In Chapter 4, you will connect this same project to the page and make the monster clickable.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Chapter 3<br/>Create game data] --> B[score, name, lives, inventory]
    B --> C[Chapter 4<br/>Connect JavaScript to the page]
    C --> D[Click the monster<br/>and update the game]
```

::: {.callout-note title="The Main Idea"}
Chapter 3 answers this question:

**What information should the game remember?**

Chapter 4 will answer the next question:

**How does JavaScript react when the player clicks something on the page?**
:::

## Think through the Monster Clicker before coding {#sec-ch03-development-flow}

| Development step | Decision for our game | Check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Build the scene structure | Show a title, monster button, message, and score inside a main card. | All four parts exist; `monster`, `message`, and `score` have distinct IDs. |
| 2. Style the scene | Reuse Chapter 2's readable card, button frame, colors, and spacing. | The monster and score are easy to find; the button has a visible keyboard focus ring. |
| 3. Program game behavior | Plan a hit that raises the score and changes the message. Prepare score, lives, treasures, and player data first. | Inspect the starting values in the console. The hit action is implemented in Chapter 4. |

For every JavaScript example in this chapter, ask **which future operation needs this value?** A score supports counting hits. Lives support tracking remaining chances. A Boolean supports a running/not-running decision. An array supports a treasure collection. An object groups player information. These small examples practice the memory part of Step 3; they do not each need a new page or stylesheet.

When a practice task changes only data, keep the existing structure and style and work on that one behavior preparation. When a task needs a new visible part, return to structure, style the new part, and then connect its behavior.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- apply **Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior** when building the starter;
- explain why games need variables;
- declare variables with `let`, `const`, and `var`;
- choose between `let` and `const` in simple programs;
- recognize number, string, Boolean, and `undefined` values;
- explain that JavaScript uses the `Number` type for both whole and decimal numbers;
- create an array to store a list of values;
- create an object to store related key-value pairs;
- change the value stored in a variable;
- build the starting data for the Monster Clicker project that will continue in Chapter 4.

## A Variable Gives a Value a Name

Imagine that your game has a score of `0`.

You could write:

```javascript
0
```

But this number does not explain what it means. Is it the score? The number of lives? The level number?

Instead, we give the value a useful name:

```javascript
let score = 0;
```

A **variable** is a named place where a program keeps a value.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Variable name<br/>score] --> B[Stored value<br/>0]
```

Read this line in pieces:

```javascript
let score = 0;
```

- `let` tells JavaScript to create a variable.
- `score` is the variable's name.
- `=` means **assign** or **store**.
- `0` is the value being stored.
- `;` marks the end of the statement.

::: {.callout-note title="Understand `=`"}
In JavaScript, `=` means **assignment**.

```javascript
score = 5;
```

means:

**Store the value `5` in `score`.**

It does not mean mathematical equality.
:::

### Use meaningful names {.unnumbered}

Compare these two variables:

```javascript
let x = 0;
```

```javascript
let score = 0;
```

Both work, but `score` tells us what the value means.

Game variables might have names such as:

```javascript
let score = 0;
let lives = 3;
let level = 1;
let playerSpeed = 5;
```

JavaScript variable names cannot contain spaces. For names with several words, JavaScript programmers often use **camelCase**:

```javascript
let playerName = "Maya";
let monsterHealth = 10;
let treasureCount = 0;
```

The first word starts with a lowercase letter. Each later word begins with a capital letter.

## Variables Can Store Different Kinds of Values

Games need to remember more than scores. A game might remember a name, a speed, whether a door is open, or a list of treasures.

The kind of value stored in a variable is called its **data type**.

### Numbers {.unnumbered}

JavaScript uses the type `Number` for ordinary numbers.

```javascript
let score = 7;
let lives = 3;
let speed = 2.5;
```

`7` and `3` are whole-number values. They are often called **integers**.

`2.5` contains a decimal part. It is often called a **floating-point** or decimal value.

But JavaScript does not normally separate these into `int` and `float` variable types. Both are JavaScript numbers.

```javascript
console.log(typeof 7);    // number
console.log(typeof 2.5);  // number
```

::: {.callout-warning title="JavaScript Is Different from Some Languages"}
In languages such as Java or C++, you may see declarations using types such as `int`, `float`, or `double`.

In JavaScript, both of these are ordinary `Number` values:

```javascript
let hits = 7;
let speed = 2.5;
```
:::

### Strings {.unnumbered}

A **string** stores text.

```javascript
let playerName = "Maya";
let monsterName = "Pixel Beast";
let message = "Get ready!";
```

String values go inside quotation marks.

Compare:

```javascript
let score = 7;     // Number
let label = "7";   // String
```

They look similar, but JavaScript treats them as different kinds of values.

### Boolean values {.unnumbered}

A **Boolean** has only two possible values:

```javascript
true
false
```

For example:

```javascript
let gameStarted = false;
let monsterVisible = true;
```

Booleans are useful for yes-or-no game states:

- Is the game running?
- Is the player alive?
- Is the door open?
- Has the treasure been collected?

Do not put quotation marks around a Boolean value:

```javascript
let gameStarted = true;    // Boolean
let word = "true";         // String
```

### `undefined`: no value yet {.unnumbered}

A variable can exist before a useful value has been stored in it.

```javascript
let playerChoice;
```

At this point, the value is `undefined`.

For beginner programs, it is usually easier to give variables a useful starting value:

```javascript
let score = 0;
let playerName = "";
let gameStarted = false;
```

## Changing a Variable

The most useful game values usually change while the game runs.

Start with:

```javascript
let score = 0;
```

Later, the game can store a new value:

```javascript
score = 1;
```

Then another:

```javascript
score = 2;
```

The variable name stays `score`, but the stored value changes.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[score = 0] --> B[score = 1]
    B --> C[score = 2]
    C --> D[score = 3]
```

A shorter way to add one is:

```javascript
score = score + 1;
```

Read it from right to left:

1. read the current value of `score`;
2. add `1`;
3. store the new value back in `score`.

If `score` begins at `0`, then:

```javascript
score = score + 1;
```

changes it to `1`.

Run it again, and the value becomes `2`.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try It in the Console"}
Try:

```javascript
let score = 0;
console.log(score);

score = score + 1;
console.log(score);

score = score + 1;
console.log(score);
```

Predict all three outputs before running the code.
:::

::: {.callout-important collapse="true" title="Advanced Study: A Shorter `+ 1`"}
JavaScript also lets you write:

```javascript
score++;
```

For now, `score = score + 1` is easier to read because it shows all three steps: read, add, and store. You will see `++` again when loops are introduced later.
:::

## Three Ways to Declare Variables: `let`, `const`, and `var`

JavaScript has three declaration keywords you will commonly see:

```javascript
let score = 0;
const gameTitle = "Monster Clicker";
var oldStyleScore = 0;
```

They all create names, but they are not used in exactly the same way.

### Use `let` when the value will be reassigned {.unnumbered}

A score changes, so `let` is a good choice:

```javascript
let score = 0;
score = 1;
score = 2;
```

Other common game examples are:

```javascript
let lives = 3;
let level = 1;
let gameStarted = false;
```

### Use `const` when the variable should keep the same value or reference {.unnumbered}

Some names do not need to point to a different value.

```javascript
const gameTitle = "Monster Clicker";
const maxLives = 3;
```

You cannot reassign a `const` variable:

```javascript
const maxLives = 3;
maxLives = 5; // Error
```

A useful beginner rule is:

> Use `const` when you do not plan to reassign the variable. Use `let` when you know the stored value must be replaced later.

### What is `var`? {.unnumbered}

Older JavaScript programs often use `var`:

```javascript
var score = 0;
```

`var` was the traditional way to declare JavaScript variables before `let` and `const` were added to the language.

You should recognize it because you may see it in older tutorials and programs.

For the games in this book, we will usually prefer `let` and `const`.

| Declaration | Beginner use in this book | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `let` | the variable will be reassigned | `let score = 0;` |
| `const` | the variable should keep the same value/reference | `const gameTitle = "Monster Clicker";` |
| `var` | recognize older JavaScript code | `var score = 0;` |

::: {.callout-note title="Book Rule"}
When writing new code:

1. Ask: **Will I reassign this variable later?**
2. If yes, use `let`.
3. If no, use `const`.
4. Recognize `var`, but you usually do not need to choose it for new code in this book.
:::

::: {.callout-important collapse="true" title="Advanced Study: Why Modern JavaScript Prefers `let` and `const`"}
`let` and `const` use **block scope**. A variable created inside a `{ }` block belongs to that block.

```javascript
{
  let bonus = 5;
  console.log(bonus);
}

// bonus cannot be used here
```

`var` follows older scoping rules and does not behave the same way inside blocks. You do not need to master scope yet, but this difference is one reason modern JavaScript usually uses `let` and `const`.
:::

## Arrays Store a List of Values

Suppose the Monster Clicker game can award several treasures:

- a coin;
- a gem;
- a key.

You could create three variables:

```javascript
const treasure1 = "coin";
const treasure2 = "gem";
const treasure3 = "key";
```

But these values belong together. An **array** stores a list in one variable.

```javascript
const treasures = ["coin", "gem", "key"];
```

Square brackets `[` and `]` mark the array. Commas separate the items.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[treasures] --> B[0: coin]
    A --> C[1: gem]
    A --> D[2: key]
```

Each item has a numbered position called an **index**.

JavaScript starts array indexes at `0`:

```javascript
console.log(treasures[0]); // coin
console.log(treasures[1]); // gem
console.log(treasures[2]); // key
```

So the first item is at index `0`, not index `1`.

### An array can change even when declared with `const` {.unnumbered}

Start with an inventory:

```javascript
const inventory = ["map"];
```

Add another item:

```javascript
inventory.push("key");
```

Now the array contains:

```text
map, key
```

This is allowed because `const` keeps the variable from being reassigned to a different array. It does not freeze the contents of the array.

This is allowed:

```javascript
const inventory = ["map"];
inventory.push("key");
```

This is not:

```javascript
const inventory = ["map"];
inventory = ["gem"]; // Error
```

You can also check how many items an array contains:

```javascript
console.log(inventory.length);
```

## Objects Store Related Information with Keys

An array is useful for an ordered list. Sometimes, however, each value needs a name.

Imagine that the Monster Clicker player has a name, score, and lives:

```javascript
const player = {
  name: "Maya",
  score: 0,
  lives: 3
};
```

This is an **object**.

An object stores related information as **key-value pairs**.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[player] --> B[name → Maya]
    A --> C[score → 0]
    A --> D[lives → 3]
```

In this object:

- `name` is a key and `"Maya"` is its value;
- `score` is a key and `0` is its value;
- `lives` is a key and `3` is its value.

You can read an object property with a dot:

```javascript
console.log(player.name);
console.log(player.score);
```

You can also change a property:

```javascript
player.score = 1;
```

Even though `player` was declared with `const`, changing one of its properties is allowed. The variable still refers to the same object.

::: {.callout-note title="Array or Object?"}
Use an **array** when you mainly need an ordered list:

```javascript
const treasures = ["coin", "gem", "key"];
```

Use an **object** when each piece of information needs a descriptive key:

```javascript
const player = {
  name: "Maya",
  score: 0,
  lives: 3
};
```
:::

::: {.callout-important collapse="true" title="Advanced Study: Object and `Map` Are Not the Same Thing"}
A JavaScript object can be used like a simple key-value collection, but JavaScript also has a separate built-in type called `Map`.

`Map` is a later topic. For now, objects are enough for storing small groups of named game information.
:::

## Build the Monster Clicker Starter

Now use the ideas from this chapter to start a project that will continue in Chapter 4.

At the end of this chapter, your game will have:

- a monster on the page;
- a place for a message;
- a place where the score will eventually appear;
- JavaScript variables that describe the game;
- an inventory array;
- a player object.

The monster will **not respond to clicks yet**. That is intentional.

Chapter 4 will introduce the missing ideas: how JavaScript finds HTML elements and how **events** tell the program that the player clicked something.

### Step 1: Build the scene structure — build the HTML game board {.unnumbered}

Sketch the title, monster, message, and score first. Create a file such as `monster-clicker.html`, or continue the Chapter 2 rehearsal page. Keep the script as a placeholder while checking this first stage:

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Monster Clicker</title>
  <style>
    /* Step 2: Style the scene rules will go here. */
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <!-- Step 1: Build the scene structure (page structure). -->
  <main class="card">
    <h1>Monster Clicker</h1>
    <button id="monster" class="monster" type="button">👾 Monster</button>
    <p id="message">The monster is waiting...</p>
    <p id="score">Score: 0</p>
  </main>

  <script>
    // Step 3: Program game behavior — prepare data; click actions come in Chapter 4.
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

You already know the HTML pieces from Chapter 2.

Notice these IDs:

```html
id="monster"
id="message"
id="score"
```

Do not write JavaScript to use them yet. Keep them in the page because **Chapter 4 will show how JavaScript uses an element's `id` to find that exact element**.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[id="monster"] --> B[Monster button]
    C[id="message"] --> D[Message paragraph]
    E[id="score"] --> F[Score paragraph]
```

::: {.callout-note title="A Preview for Chapter 4"}
The `id` values are like unique labels attached to HTML elements.

In Chapter 4, JavaScript will use those labels to find the monster, message, and score on the page.
:::

### Step 2: Style the scene — reuse the page design {.unnumbered}

The structure is ready. Put this familiar CSS inside the head's `<style>` element, replacing its placeholder comment. These are Chapter 2's styling ideas; the shared `.monster` class will also work when you add more monsters later.

```css
* { box-sizing: border-box; }
body {
  margin: 0;
  min-height: 100vh;
  display: grid;
  place-items: center;
  background: #eef7ff;
  color: #17243b;
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
}
.card {
  width: min(92%, 620px);
  padding: 24px;
  border: 3px solid #17243b;
  border-radius: 20px;
  background: white;
}
.monster {
  padding: 18px;
  border: 2px solid #17243b;
  border-radius: 14px;
  background: #e7dcff;
  font: inherit;
  cursor: pointer;
}
.monster:focus-visible {
  outline: 4px solid #ffe48a;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}
#message { min-height: 1.5em; }
```

Save and refresh. Check the card, monster, message, and score before adding JavaScript. If you continued the Chapter 2 page, you can instead keep its linked `styles.css`; the development step is the same. This chapter embeds CSS only to keep the complete example in one file.

### Step 3: Program game behavior — prepare memory for game actions {.unnumbered}

Write the intended rule first: **When the monster is hit, add one to the score and update the message.** That action needs a score to remember between hits. Prepare the starting data now; Chapter 4 will implement the event and display changes. Styling a button does not connect that operation.

The substeps below all belong to this behavior-preparation stage.

#### Prepare the basic game variables {.unnumbered}

Inside the `<script>` block, add:

```javascript
const gameTitle = "Monster Clicker";
const monsterName = "Pixel Beast";

let score = 0;
let lives = 3;
let gameStarted = false;
```

Why are the declarations different?

```javascript
const gameTitle = "Monster Clicker";
const monsterName = "Pixel Beast";
```

These values are not expected to be reassigned during this simple game, so `const` is a good choice.

```javascript
let score = 0;
let lives = 3;
let gameStarted = false;
```

These values may change while the game runs, so `let` is a good choice.

#### Prepare a treasure list {.unnumbered}

Add an array:

```javascript
const treasures = ["coin", "gem", "key"];
```

Later, the game could choose one of these rewards when the monster is hit.

For now, inspect the values in the browser console:

```javascript
console.log(treasures[0]);
console.log(treasures[1]);
console.log(treasures[2]);
```

#### Group player information in an object {.unnumbered}

Add:

```javascript
const player = {
  name: "Maya",
  score: 0,
  lives: 3
};
```

Then try:

```javascript
console.log(player.name);
console.log(player.score);
console.log(player.lives);
```

This object shows another way the game could organize related data.

For the first version of Monster Clicker, Chapter 4 will continue to use the simpler variable:

```javascript
let score = 0;
```

That keeps the first event example easy to follow. The `player` object gives you a preview of how larger games can organize several related values together.

#### Practice changing the score in memory {.unnumbered}

Before a click can change the score automatically, practice changing it yourself:

```javascript
console.log(score); // 0

score = score + 1;
console.log(score); // 1

score = score + 1;
console.log(score); // 2
```

The number on the web page still says:

```text
Score: 0
```

Why?

Because the JavaScript variable and the HTML paragraph are not connected yet.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[JavaScript memory<br/>score = 2] -. not connected yet .-> B[HTML display<br/>Score: 0]
```

This is the exact problem Chapter 4 will solve.

::: {.callout-note title="Important: Memory and Display Are Different"}
The variable:

```javascript
let score = 0;
```

stores information in JavaScript memory.

The HTML:

```html
<p id="score">Score: 0</p>
```

displays text on the page.

Changing one does not automatically change the other. In Chapter 4, you will learn how JavaScript finds the paragraph and updates it.
:::

## Complete Chapter 3 Starter Code

Read this complete example in our development order: locate the **scene structure** in the body, then its **style** in the head, then the data preparing its **behaviors** in the script. The head comes before the body in HTML file order; that does not change the thinking strategy. A runnable copy is in `workspace/chapter3/starter.html`.

```html

  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

      outline: 4px solid #ffe48a;

    }

  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <!-- Step 1: Build the scene structure (page structure). -->
  <main class="card">
    <h1>Monster Clicker</h1>

    <p id="message">The monster is waiting...</p>
    <p id="score">Score: 0</p>
  </main>

  <script>
```

When you open the page:

- the monster appears;

That last point is not a bug. It marks your progress.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[Build the scene structure<br/>HTML page elements] --> S[Style the scene<br/>CSS presentation]
    S --> B[Program game behavior: Chapter 3<br/>Prepare game data and memory]
```

## Exercises

Use **Structure → Style → Behavior** as a check before each task. The focus below identifies the stage you are practicing. For reading or prediction tasks, trace or explain the result; you do not need a new page or visual redesign.

### Exercise 1: Name the parts of a declaration

**Flow focus:** Program game behavior: identify the memory a future score action will change; keep the existing scene and style.

Look at:

```javascript
let score = 0;
```

Identify:

4. the starting value.

### Exercise 2: Choose `let` or `const`

**Flow focus:** Program game behavior: decide which values future actions can replace and which bindings stay fixed.

Choose the better declaration for each value.

2. The title `"Monster Clicker"`.
3. The current level, which can change.
4. An array named `treasures` that will remain the same array.
5. The maximum number of lives, which does not change.

### Exercise 4: Identify the data type

**Flow focus:** Program game behavior: identify the kinds of data available to game operations.

For each value, identify whether it is a **Number**, **String**, or **Boolean**.

```javascript
2.5
"10"
"Pixel Beast"
true
false
```

### Exercise 5: Predict the score

**Flow focus:** Program game behavior: predict successive updates to memory before checking the output.

What is printed?

```javascript
score = score + 1;
```

### Exercise 6: Read an array

### Exercise 7: Read an object

### Exercise 8: Memory versus page display

Suppose the page contains:

and JavaScript later runs:

# Make the Page React: DOM Elements and Click Events {#sec-ch04}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[GAME 04 | Click the Monster]{.game-title}

[DOM]{.skill-chip} [Events]{.skill-chip} [JavaScript]{.skill-chip}

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="Structure → Style → Behavior" icon="false"}

**Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior.**

- **Build the scene structure:** Identify or add the character, buttons, images, and message elements with unique IDs.
- **Style the scene:** Keep controls recognizable and text readable; default browser styling is enough for a small test.
- **Behavior:** Find the elements, attach one event handler, and compare its actual response with your prediction.

Use this plan for the examples and exercises below. Reuse parts that already work; change only what the task needs. After each step, predict one result and check it.

:::


## Overview

In Chapter 2, you used **HTML** to put things on a page and **CSS** to change how they look. In Chapter 3, you learned how JavaScript stores values using variables such as `const` and `let`.

Now we can connect JavaScript to the web page itself. A game needs to know **which thing on the page** JavaScript should work with and **when something happens** to that thing.

Imagine a monster button on the screen. Two questions must be answered before JavaScript can make it part of a game:

1. **How can JavaScript find the monster on the page?**
2. **How can JavaScript know when the player clicks it?**

Those two questions introduce two of the most important ideas in browser programming:

- the **DOM**, which lets JavaScript find and change page elements;
- **events**, which let JavaScript react to things that happen.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[HTML creates the page] --> B[Browser builds the DOM]
    B --> C[JavaScript finds an element]
    D[Player clicks] --> E[Click event]
    E --> F[JavaScript reacts]
    F --> C
```

By the end of this chapter, one ordinary web page will become your first interactive web game.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- explain what an **HTML element** is;
- explain why the HTML `id` attribute gives JavaScript a way to identify one element;
- describe the DOM as the browser's JavaScript-friendly representation of the page;
- connect `id="..."` in HTML to the string used by `document.getElementById("...")`;
- explain what an **event** is;
- distinguish normal top-to-bottom execution from **event-driven execution**;
- connect a `click` event to a JavaScript function with `addEventListener()`;
- trace the flow from **page setup → waiting → event → handler → DOM change**;
- recognize that keyboard, input, and other events follow the same event-listener pattern.

## From HTML Elements to DOM Elements

Start with a small page:

```html
<h1>Click the Monster!</h1>
<button id="monster">👾 Monster</button>
<p id="message">Can you catch it?</p>
```

The browser shows three visible pieces:

- a heading;
- a button;
- a paragraph.

Each piece created by an HTML tag is an **HTML element**.

For example:

```html
<button id="monster">👾 Monster</button>
```

This creates a button element. The attribute `id="monster"` gives that element a unique name on the page.

::: {.callout-note title="Understand"}
An **element** is one part of a web page. Headings, paragraphs, buttons, images, and input boxes are all examples of elements.
:::

### The browser creates a page model {.unnumbered}

When the browser reads HTML, it does more than draw words and buttons on the screen. It also creates an organized representation of those elements in memory.

That representation is called the **Document Object Model**, usually shortened to **DOM**.

For beginners, you can think of the DOM as the browser's **live map of the page**.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    D[document] --> H[h1: Click the Monster!]
    D --> B[button: monster]
    D --> P[p: message]
```

The HTML file is the code you wrote. The DOM is the live page structure the browser created from that code.

JavaScript works with this live DOM while the page is running.

::: {.callout-note title="HTML File vs. DOM"}
**HTML file:** the source code saved on your computer.

**DOM:** the browser's live representation of the page after it reads the HTML.

JavaScript usually changes the DOM while the program runs. It does not rewrite your saved HTML file.
:::

## The `id`: The Link Between HTML and JavaScript

Before JavaScript can change a monster, button, message, or picture, it must know **which element you mean**.

HTML gives us an important attribute for this job: `id`.

Look closely at this button:

```html
<button id="monster">👾 Monster</button>
```

The whole thing is a `button` element. Inside its opening tag, this part:

```html
id="monster"
```

gives that element an **ID value** of `monster`.

Think of an ID like a name tag attached to one object on the page.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[HTML button element] --> B[id="monster"]
    B --> C[Unique label: monster]
```

::: {.callout-note title="Understand: Attribute Name and Attribute Value"}
In:

```html
id="monster"
```

- `id` is the **attribute name**;
- `monster` is the **attribute value**.

The value is written inside quotation marks in the HTML.
:::

### Why the ID matters {.unnumbered}

A page may contain many buttons, paragraphs, and images.

```html
<button id="monster">👾 Monster</button>
<button id="startButton">Start</button>
<p id="message">Can you catch it?</p>
```

If JavaScript only said, “Give me a button,” which button should the browser choose?

The ID gives JavaScript a precise way to identify one element.

For this HTML:

```html
<button id="monster">👾 Monster</button>
```

JavaScript can ask:

```javascript
const monster = document.getElementById("monster");
```

The string inside `getElementById()` must match the HTML ID value.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    H[HTML] --> I[id="monster"]
    I -->|same value| J[getElementById("monster")]
    J --> D[DOM button element]
    D --> V[const monster]
```

This connection is so important that it is worth reading both directions:

```text
HTML:       id="monster"
                     ↓ same text
JavaScript: getElementById("monster")
```

The word `monster` is **not special JavaScript vocabulary**. You chose that ID in the HTML, and JavaScript uses the same value to find the element.

::: {.callout-warning title="The Two Names Do Not Have to Match"}
This is valid:

```html
<button id="monster">👾 Monster</button>
```

```javascript
const enemyButton = document.getElementById("monster");
```

There are two different names here:

- `"monster"` is the **HTML ID value** JavaScript searches for;
- `enemyButton` is the **JavaScript variable name** that stores the found DOM element.

Using the same word for both can be easier for beginners, but JavaScript does not require it.
:::

### Step by step: from HTML to a JavaScript variable {.unnumbered}

Start with the HTML:

```html
<p id="message">Can you catch it?</p>
```

**Step 1 — HTML gives the element an ID.**

```text
id value = message
```

**Step 2 — The browser creates a DOM element.**

The DOM element keeps information about that paragraph, including its ID.

**Step 3 — JavaScript asks the DOM for that ID.**

```javascript
document.getElementById("message")
```

**Step 4 — The browser returns the matching DOM element.**

**Step 5 — A variable stores the returned element.**

```javascript
const message = document.getElementById("message");
```

Because Chapter 3 introduced variables, you can read this as an assignment:

> Put the DOM element whose ID is `message` into the constant named `message`.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[HTML source] --> B["<p id='message'>"]
    B --> C[Browser builds DOM]
    C --> D[DOM paragraph with id message]
    E["getElementById('message')"] --> F{Matching ID?}
    D --> F
    F -->|Yes| G[Return DOM element]
    G --> H[Store it in const message]
```

### IDs should identify one element {.unnumbered}

An HTML `id` should be unique on the page.

Good:

```html
<button id="monster">Monster</button>
<p id="message">Ready!</p>
```

Avoid giving two different elements the same ID:

```html
<button id="monster">Monster 1</button>
<button id="monster">Monster 2</button>
```

If several game objects need to belong to the same group, later you will learn other ways to select groups of elements. For now, use one unique ID for each element JavaScript needs to find directly.

::: {.callout-warning title="IDs Must Match Exactly"}
This HTML:

```html
<button id="monster">Monster</button>
```

matches:

```javascript
document.getElementById("monster")
```

but it does **not** match:

```javascript
document.getElementById("Monster")
document.getElementById("monsters")
document.getElementById("monsterButton")
```

The browser searches for the exact ID value you provide.
:::

### What does `document` mean? {.unnumbered}

In browser JavaScript, `document` represents the current web page's DOM.

So:

```javascript
document.getElementById("monster")
```

can be read as:

> In the current page, get the element whose ID value is `monster`.

This gives us our first reusable browser-programming pattern:

```text
Give an HTML element an ID
        ↓
Use the same ID in getElementById()
        ↓
Store the returned DOM element in a variable
```

## A DOM Element Can Be Changed

Finding an element matters because JavaScript can now do something with it.

For example, this line changes the paragraph text:

```javascript
message.textContent = "Great hit!";
```

`textContent` means the text stored inside that DOM element.

Before JavaScript runs:

```html
<p id="message">Can you catch it?</p>
```

After this JavaScript runs:

```javascript
message.textContent = "Great hit!";
```

the browser shows:

```text
Great hit!
```

The saved HTML file has not changed. The browser changed the **DOM**, so the player sees the new text immediately.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try It"}
Open the browser console on a simple page and try:

```javascript
document.getElementById("message").textContent = "Hello from JavaScript!";
```

If the page has an element with `id="message"`, its text changes immediately.
:::

This gives us our first important game pattern:

```text
Find an element → Change the element
```

But a game should not change everything immediately. Usually it should wait for the **player**.

That brings us to events.

## 4.4 What Is an Event?

An **event** is something that happens while the page is running.

Many events come from the player:

- clicking or tapping;
- pressing a key;
- moving the mouse;
- typing in an input box;
- changing a selection.

Some events come from the browser or program:

- the page finishes loading;
- a timer finishes;
- an animation frame is ready.

For now, we will begin with the easiest event to see: **click**.

### Normal programs often run top to bottom {.unnumbered}

When beginners first learn programming, code often looks like a fixed sequence:

```javascript
const playerName = "Mia";
const score = 0;
console.log(playerName);
console.log(score);
```

The computer begins at the top and executes the statements in order.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[Start] --> B[Run statement 1]
    B --> C[Run statement 2]
    C --> D[Run statement 3]
    D --> E[Finish]
```

That model is useful, but an interactive web game has another kind of execution.

## Event-Driven Programming: Set Up, Then Wait

A web page cannot know **when** the player will click.

The player might click immediately, five seconds later, or never.

So an event-driven program usually has two phases:

1. **Setup phase** — JavaScript runs code that prepares the page and registers event listeners.
2. **Waiting-and-response phase** — the browser waits. When an event occurs, it runs the connected handler function.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[Page starts] --> B[Run setup code]
    B --> C[Find DOM elements]
    C --> D[Register event listeners]
    D --> E[Browser waits]
    E --> F{Did an event happen?}
    F -->|No| E
    F -->|Yes: click| G[Run click handler]
    G --> H[Change game state or DOM]
    H --> E
```

The important difference is the loop back to **waiting**.

The whole JavaScript file does not restart after every click. Instead, the browser remembers the event listener and calls the connected function whenever the event happens.

::: {.callout-note title="Event-Driven Does Not Mean Random Order"}
The browser still executes each function's statements in order.

What changes is **when a function begins**. An event handler starts because an event occurred, not simply because it was the next line in the original file.
:::

### Compare the two execution models {.unnumbered}

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    subgraph Normal[Simple sequential program]
      A1[Start] --> A2[Statement A] --> A3[Statement B] --> A4[Statement C] --> A5[End]
    end

    subgraph EventDriven[Event-driven web program]
      B1[Setup] --> B2[Register listener] --> B3[Wait]
      B3 -->|event| B4[Run handler]
      B4 --> B3
    end
```

This is a major idea in web games: **the program spends much of its time waiting for events and reacting to them**.

## Listening for a Click Event

Consider this game rule:

> When the player clicks the monster, show “Great hit!”

It contains two parts:

1. **Event:** the player clicks the monster.
2. **Event handler:** the code that responds to the click.

First, JavaScript gets the element:

```javascript
const monster = document.getElementById("monster");
```

Then we define the response function:

```javascript
function hitMonster() {
  message.textContent = "Great hit!";
}
```

Finally, we connect the element, event type, and function:

```javascript
monster.addEventListener("click", hitMonster);
```

Read it like this:

> On the `monster` DOM element, listen for a `click`. When that click occurs, run `hitMonster`.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[DOM element: monster] --> D[Event listener]
    B[Event type: click] --> D
    C[Handler: hitMonster] --> D
    D --> E[Browser remembers the connection]
    F[Player clicks later] --> G[click event occurs]
    G --> E
    E --> H[Browser calls hitMonster]
```

### Why `hitMonster` has no parentheses {.unnumbered}

Use:

```javascript
monster.addEventListener("click", hitMonster);
```

not:

```javascript
monster.addEventListener("click", hitMonster());
```

`hitMonster` gives the browser the function so it can run it **later** when the event happens.

`hitMonster()` means **run the function now** while the setup code is executing.

## The Same Event Pattern Works for Other Events

The click event is only the first example. The same structure can be reused for many events.

```text
DOM element + event type + handler function
```

For a click:

```javascript
monster.addEventListener("click", hitMonster);
```

For typing into an input box:

```javascript
nameBox.addEventListener("input", updateName);
```

For pressing a key:

```javascript
document.addEventListener("keydown", movePlayer);
```

The event names are different, but the mental model is the same.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[Something happens] --> B{Which event?}
    B -->|click| C[Run click handler]
    B -->|keydown| D[Run keyboard handler]
    B -->|input| E[Run input handler]
    C --> F[Update game]
    D --> F
    E --> F
    F --> G[Wait for the next event]
```

You do **not** need to memorize all event types now. The important idea is that browsers report events, and your program chooses which events to listen for.

### Put the DOM and event ideas together {.unnumbered}

The full browser-game pattern is:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[HTML gives element an id] --> B[Browser builds DOM]
    B --> C[JavaScript gets element by id]
    C --> D[JavaScript registers event listener]
    D --> E[Browser waits]
    E --> F[Player action creates event]
    F --> G[Browser runs handler function]
    G --> H[Handler changes game state or DOM]
    H --> E
```

Or remember it as:

```text
ID → Get element → Listen → Wait → Event → Handler → Change → Wait again
```

## Build the First Click Game

Now put everything into one page.

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Click the Monster</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Click the Monster!</h1>

  <button id="monster">👾 Monster</button>
  <p id="message">Can you catch it?</p>

  <script>
    const monster = document.getElementById("monster");
    const message = document.getElementById("message");

    function hitMonster() {
      message.textContent = "Great hit!";
    }

    monster.addEventListener("click", hitMonster);
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

### What happens when the page opens? {.unnumbered}

The browser:

1. reads the HTML;
2. builds DOM elements for the heading, button, and paragraph;
3. reaches the `<script>`;
4. finds the `monster` and `message` DOM elements;
5. creates the `hitMonster` function;
6. attaches a click listener to the monster;
7. enters the waiting phase.

Nothing says “Great hit!” yet because the handler has not been called. The browser is waiting for a click event.

### What happens when the player clicks? {.unnumbered}

The browser:

1. detects a `click` event on the monster;
2. sees that a click listener is attached;
3. runs `hitMonster()`;
4. changes `message.textContent`;
5. redraws the page with the new message.

That is your first event-driven game interaction.

## A Picture Can Receive Events Too

A click event is not only for buttons.

Any DOM element can receive events, including an image.

```html
<img id="gem" src="gem.svg" alt="Purple game gem" width="96">
<p id="message">Click the gem.</p>
```

JavaScript can find the image:

```javascript
const gem = document.getElementById("gem");
const message = document.getElementById("message");
```

Then listen for its click:

```javascript
function collectGem() {
  message.textContent = "You collected the gem!";
}

gem.addEventListener("click", collectGem);
```

The important idea is not “buttons can be clicked.”

The important idea is:

> JavaScript can find a DOM element and listen for events on that element.

That is much more powerful. Later, game characters, cards, menu items, pictures, and parts of a game screen can all become interactive.

## One Mental Model to Remember

If this chapter feels like many new words, remember this simple model:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[HTML element] --> B[DOM element]
    B --> C[JavaScript gets it]
    D[Player action] --> E[Event]
    E --> F[Event listener]
    F --> G[Function runs]
    G --> H[DOM changes]
```

Or say it in one sentence:

> **JavaScript gets a DOM element, listens for an event, and changes the page when that event happens.**

::: {.callout-important collapse="true" title="Advanced Study: What If JavaScript Cannot Find the Element?"}
If this code cannot find a matching element:

```javascript
const monster = document.getElementById("monster");
```

JavaScript receives a special value called `null`.

This can happen when:

- the ID is misspelled;
- the element does not have that ID;
- JavaScript runs before the browser has created that element.

For now, keep the `<script>` near the bottom of `<body>`, after the elements your JavaScript needs. That way, the browser creates those DOM elements before JavaScript searches for them.
:::
