# Let the Monster Clicker Make Decisions {#sec-ch05}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[GAME 05 | Monster Clicker: Decisions]{.game-title}

[Branches]{.skill-chip} [Comparisons]{.skill-chip} [Game Rules]{.skill-chip}

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="Structure → Style → Behavior" icon="false"}

**Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior.**

- **Build the scene structure:** Identify the monster, special-action controls, score, and message; add a control only if the rule needs one.
- **Style the scene:** Make action labels, costs, and success/refusal messages easy to distinguish.
- **Behavior:** Implement the conditions and score changes, then test below, at, and above each threshold.

Use this plan for the examples and exercises below. Reuse parts that already work; change only what the task needs. After each step, predict one result and check it.

:::


## Overview

In Chapter 3, you prepared the game’s **memory** with variables such as a score. In Chapter 4, you connected that memory to the page and increased the score when the player clicked the monster.

Now the game needs something new: **rules**.

A real game does not always do the same thing. It asks questions:

- Is the score high enough for a power move?
- Has the player reached a new level?
- Has the player won?
- Should the game show encouragement or a victory message?

JavaScript answers these questions with **conditions** and **branches**. A branch lets the program choose one path or another.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Player clicks monster] --> B[Score changes]
    B --> C{What is the score?}
    C -->|Less than 5| D[Keep going!]
    C -->|5 to 9| E[Monster is nervous!]
    C -->|10 or more| F[You win!]
```

The game is still the same project. We are not throwing away Chapters 3 and 4. We are **upgrading** them.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- explain what a **condition** is;
- use comparison operators such as `===`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, and `>=`;
- write an `if` statement;
- choose between two paths with `if` and `else`;
- choose among several paths with `if`, `else if`, and `else`;
- use branches to create rules for the Monster Clicker game.

## 5.1 From Memory to Decisions

At the end of Chapter 4, your clicker had code like this:

```javascript
let score = 0;

function hitMonster() {
  score = score + 1;
  scoreText.textContent = "Score: " + score;
}
```

Every click does exactly the same thing:

1. add 1 to `score`;
2. show the new score.

But suppose you want the game to say **"You reached 5 hits!"** when the score reaches 5.

Now the program must ask a question:

> Is the score equal to 5?

That kind of yes-or-no question is called a **condition**.

## 5.2 Conditions Become `true` or `false`

A condition is an expression that JavaScript can answer with either:

- `true` — yes;
- `false` — no.

For example:

```javascript
score === 5
```

If `score` is 5, this condition is `true`.

If `score` is 3, this condition is `false`.

::: {.callout-note title="Important: `=` and `===` Have Different Jobs"}

These symbols look similar, but they do different jobs.

```javascript
score = 5;      // store 5 in score
score === 5     // ask: is score equal to 5?
```

Use `=` to **assign** a value.

Use `===` to **compare** values.

:::

Here are several useful comparison operators:

| Operator | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `===` | equal to | `score === 5` |
| `!==` | not equal to | `score !== 5` |
| `>` | greater than | `score > 5` |
| `<` | less than | `score < 5` |
| `>=` | greater than or equal to | `score >= 5` |
| `<=` | less than or equal to | `score <= 5` |

::: {.callout-tip title="Try It: Predict Before Running"}

Suppose `score` is 7. Decide whether each condition is `true` or `false`.

```javascript
score === 7
score > 10
score >= 5
score < 7
score !== 3
```

:::

## 5.3 Your First Branch with `if`

An `if` statement tells JavaScript:

> If this condition is true, run this code.

```javascript
if (score === 5) {
  message.textContent = "You reached 5 hits!";
}
```

Read it from top to bottom:

1. `if` starts a decision.
2. `(score === 5)` is the condition.
3. `{` and `}` surround the code that belongs to this branch.
4. The message changes only when the condition is `true`.

Add it to the Monster Clicker:

```javascript
function hitMonster() {
  score = score + 1;
  scoreText.textContent = "Score: " + score;

  if (score === 5) {
    message.textContent = "You reached 5 hits!";
  }
}
```

Now the game behaves differently on one special click.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[Monster clicked] --> B[Add 1 to score]
    B --> C{score === 5?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Show milestone message]
    C -->|No| E[Do nothing extra]
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch Out: The Condition Goes Inside Parentheses"}

Write:

```javascript
if (score === 5) {
```

not:

```javascript
if score === 5 {
```

JavaScript needs the parentheses around the condition.

:::

## 5.4 Choose Between Two Paths with `if` and `else`

Sometimes the game should do one thing when a condition is true and something different when it is false.

Suppose the monster should react differently before and after 5 hits.

```javascript
if (score < 5) {
  message.textContent = "Keep clicking!";
} else {
  message.textContent = "The monster is getting nervous!";
}
```

There are now two possible paths:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A{score < 5?} -->|Yes| B[Keep clicking!]
    A -->|No| C[Monster is getting nervous!]
```

Notice that `else` does not need another condition. It means:

> If the first condition was false, do this instead.

### Put it into the click function

```javascript
function hitMonster() {
  score = score + 1;
  scoreText.textContent = "Score: " + score;

  if (score < 5) {
    message.textContent = "Keep clicking!";
  } else {
    message.textContent = "The monster is getting nervous!";
  }
}
```

This is already more game-like because the response changes as the player makes progress.

## 5.5 Choose Among Several Paths with `else if`

Games often need more than two choices.

For our Monster Clicker, let us create three stages:

- score 1–4: **Keep clicking!**
- score 5–9: **The monster is getting nervous!**
- score 10 or more: **You win!**

Use `else if` for the middle choice:

```javascript
if (score < 5) {
  message.textContent = "Keep clicking!";
} else if (score < 10) {
  message.textContent = "The monster is getting nervous!";
} else {
  message.textContent = "You win!";
}
```

JavaScript checks the branches **from top to bottom**.

If `score` is 3:

1. `score < 5` is true;
2. JavaScript uses the first branch;
3. it skips the rest.

If `score` is 7:

1. `score < 5` is false;
2. `score < 10` is true;
3. JavaScript uses the second branch.

If `score` is 12:

1. `score < 5` is false;
2. `score < 10` is false;
3. `else` runs.

::: {.callout-note title="Why Does the Middle Branch Mean 5 Through 9?"}

Look at this code again:

```javascript
if (score < 5) {
  // 0 through 4
} else if (score < 10) {
  // 5 through 9
}
```

The second branch is checked only after JavaScript already knows that `score < 5` is false.

So when JavaScript reaches `score < 10`, the score must already be 5 or more.

That is why the middle branch covers 5 through 9.

:::

## 5.6 Use a Branch to Enforce a Game Rule

Chapter 4 ended with a challenge about spending points without letting the score become negative. Branches solve that problem.

Imagine a **Power Hit** costs 5 points.

The game should ask:

> Does the player have at least 5 points?

```javascript
if (score >= 5) {
  score = score - 5;
  message.textContent = "POWER HIT! You spent 5 points.";
} else {
  message.textContent = "You need 5 points for a Power Hit.";
}
```

This branch protects the game rule. The score cannot drop below zero because subtraction happens only when `score >= 5` is true.

::: {.callout-tip title="Game Design Idea"}

A branch is more than JavaScript syntax. It is how you turn a **game rule** into code.

Rule in words:

> A Power Hit costs 5 points.

Rule in JavaScript:

```javascript
if (score >= 5) {
  score = score - 5;
}
```

:::

## 5.7 Build the Complete Game: Monster Clicker with Levels

Now combine what you built across three chapters.

- Chapter 3: the game remembers a score.
- Chapter 4: the monster listens for a click and updates the score.
- Chapter 5: the game makes decisions using that score.

[COMPLETE EXAMPLE]{.code-label}

```html
<!doctype html>
<html>
<body>
  <h1>Monster Clicker</h1>

  <button id="monster">👾 Hit the monster</button>
  <button id="power">⚡ Power Hit (-5 points)</button>

  <p id="score">Score: 0</p>
  <p id="message">Start clicking the monster!</p>

  <script>
    let score = 0;

    const monster = document.getElementById("monster");
    const power = document.getElementById("power");
    const scoreText = document.getElementById("score");
    const message = document.getElementById("message");

    function showGameState() {
      scoreText.textContent = "Score: " + score;

      if (score < 5) {
        message.textContent = "Keep clicking!";
      } else if (score < 10) {
        message.textContent = "The monster is getting nervous!";
      } else {
        message.textContent = "You reached Monster Master level!";
      }
    }

    function hitMonster() {
      score = score + 1;
      showGameState();
    }

    function powerHit() {
      if (score >= 5) {
        score = score - 5;
        scoreText.textContent = "Score: " + score;
        message.textContent = "POWER HIT! You spent 5 points.";
      } else {
        message.textContent = "You need 5 points for a Power Hit.";
      }
    }

    monster.addEventListener("click", hitMonster);
    power.addEventListener("click", powerHit);
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

Open `workspace/chapter5-monster-decisions/index.html` to try the complete example, or save the code above as `index.html`.

### Trace one game

Suppose the player starts at 0.

1. Click the monster four times. The score becomes 4 and the message says **Keep clicking!**
2. Click one more time. The score becomes 5 and the message changes to **The monster is getting nervous!**
3. Click **Power Hit**. Because `score >= 5` is true, the game spends 5 points and the score returns to 0.
4. Click **Power Hit** again. Now `score >= 5` is false, so the game refuses the move.
5. Build the score to 10. The message changes to **You reached Monster Master level!**

That is branching in action: the same button can lead to different results because the game checks its current state first.

## 5.8 Reading Branches Like a Game Designer

When you see a branch, translate it into a rule written in plain language.

```javascript
if (score >= 10) {
  message.textContent = "You win!";
}
```

Plain-language rule:

> If the player has 10 or more points, show the winning message.

Now go the other direction. Start with a rule:

> If the player has fewer than 3 points, the shield cannot be used.

One possible branch is:

```javascript
if (score < 3) {
  message.textContent = "Not enough points for a shield.";
}
```

This skill becomes very important as games grow. Collision rules, health rules, timers, lives, levels, and winning conditions all depend on decisions.

::: {.callout-important collapse="true" title="Advanced Study: Combining Conditions"}

Sometimes one rule needs more than one condition.

Use `&&` to mean **AND**:

```javascript
if (score >= 5 && score < 10) {
  message.textContent = "Level 2";
}
```

Both conditions must be true.

Use `||` to mean **OR**:

```javascript
if (score === 5 || score === 10) {
  message.textContent = "Milestone reached!";
}
```

At least one condition must be true.

You do not need these operators for the main Monster Clicker yet, but you will see them again in larger games.

:::

### Exercise 5: Add a milestone

**Flow focus:** Program game behavior: reuse the score and message, then test the milestone and its neighboring scores.

Modify the Monster Clicker so the message says **"Halfway there!"** when the score is exactly 5.

## Challenges

### Challenge 1: Add More Monster Levels

**Structure:** Reuse the monster, score, and message areas. **Style:** Make each level message distinguishable while keeping the existing layout. **Behavior:** Define the four ranges and test each boundary and a value between boundaries.

Create at least four score ranges instead of three. For example:

- 0–4: Rookie
- 5–9: Hunter
- 10–19: Monster Master
- 20 or more: Legend

Choose your own messages.

### Challenge 2: Create a Healing Rule

**Structure:** Add a Heal button and reuse the score/message areas. **Style:** Label its cost clearly and make success/refusal feedback readable. **Behavior:** Implement the spending rule and test scores below, at, and above the cost.

Add a button named **Heal** that costs 3 points.

The button should:

- subtract 3 points only when the player has enough points;
- never let the score become negative;
- show a different message when the player cannot afford the action.

### Challenge 3: Design Your Own Rule

**Structure:** Identify which existing parts your new rule uses; add a part only if needed. **Style:** Plan the visible feedback that tells the player the rule occurred. **Behavior:** Write the rule in words, implement its branch, and test both permitted and refused cases.

Invent one new rule for Monster Clicker.

Write the rule first in plain language. Then turn it into an `if`, `if/else`, or `if/else if/else` statement.

Examples of ideas:

- a bonus at a certain score;
- a warning after too many clicks;
- a special move that needs points;
- a new monster level;
- a victory condition.

# Repeat Game Actions with Loops {#sec-ch06}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[GAME 06 | Monster Swarm]{.game-title}

[Loops]{.skill-chip} [Arrays]{.skill-chip} [Repeated actions]{.skill-chip}

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="Structure → Style → Behavior" icon="false"}

**Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior.**

- **Build the scene structure:** Group the monster buttons and give each a unique ID; list those IDs in the collection.
- **Style the scene:** Use one shared monster class, wrapping, and spacing for the whole group.
- **Behavior:** Use a loop to connect or process the collection; test the first, last, and newly added monster.

Use this plan for the examples and exercises below. Reuse parts that already work; change only what the task needs. After each step, predict one result and check it.

:::


## Overview

In Chapter 3, you prepared a `score` variable so the game could remember hits. In Chapter 4, you made one monster react to a click and update that score. In Chapter 5, you added **branches** so the game could make decisions from that score.

Now the monster has called for backup.

Instead of one monster, the game will have several monsters. We *could* write the same JavaScript again and again for every monster, but that becomes tedious very quickly. A **loop** lets JavaScript repeat a block of code for us.

This chapter grows the same Monster Clicker game one more step:

```text
Chapter 3: prepare memory for the score
       ↓
Chapter 4: click a monster and update the score
       ↓
Chapter 5: make decisions from the score
       ↓
Chapter 6: repeat actions for many monsters
```

The main idea is simple:

> A branch chooses **which code** should run. A loop chooses **how many times** code should run.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Several monsters] --> B[Array of monster IDs]
    B --> C[Loop through the array]
    C --> D[Find each monster]
    D --> E[Connect the click event]
```

By the end of the chapter, one small loop will replace several nearly identical lines of JavaScript.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- explain why programs use loops;
- identify the three main parts of a `for` loop;
- trace how a loop variable changes during repetition;
- use `.length` so a loop matches the size of an array;
- loop through an array by using an index;
- use a loop to connect click events to several game elements;
- distinguish a loop from a branch;
- recognize how a loop can accidentally run forever.

## 6.1 Why Do We Need a Loop?

Imagine that our Monster Clicker now has three monsters:

```html
<button id="slime">Slime</button>
<button id="bat">Bat</button>
<button id="ghost">Ghost</button>
```

We already know how to connect one monster to the `hitMonster()` function:

```javascript
const slime = document.getElementById("slime");
slime.addEventListener("click", hitMonster);
```

For three monsters, we could repeat the same idea:

```javascript
const slime = document.getElementById("slime");
const bat = document.getElementById("bat");
const ghost = document.getElementById("ghost");

slime.addEventListener("click", hitMonster);
bat.addEventListener("click", hitMonster);
ghost.addEventListener("click", hitMonster);
```

This works, but notice the pattern. We are doing almost the same job three times.

```text
find a monster → connect its click event
find a monster → connect its click event
find a monster → connect its click event
```

A **loop** is useful when a program needs to repeat a pattern.

::: {.callout-note title="Loop Mental Model"}
A loop says:

**Repeat this block of code while a rule says to keep going.**
:::

A loop does not mean that every game must constantly repeat forever. It can repeat exactly 3 times, 10 times, or once for every item in a list.

## 6.2 Your First `for` Loop

A common JavaScript loop is the **`for` loop**.

Here is a small example:

```javascript
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  console.log("A monster appeared!");
}
```

This prints the same message three times.

The first line may look strange at first:

```javascript
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
```

A `for` loop has three important parts inside the parentheses:

```text
for ( START ; KEEP-GOING TEST ; CHANGE )
```

For our example:

```text
for ( let i = 0 ; i < 3 ; i++ )
      ─────────   ─────   ───
        start      test   change
```

### Start: `let i = 0`

```javascript
let i = 0
```

The loop creates a variable named `i` and starts it at `0`.

Programmers often use `i` as a short name for **index**. An index is a position number. You will use indexes with arrays later in this chapter.

### Keep-going test: `i < 3`

```javascript
i < 3
```

Before each repetition, JavaScript checks this condition.

- If it is `true`, the loop body runs.
- If it is `false`, the loop stops.

### Change: `i++`

```javascript
i++
```

This adds `1` to `i` after each repetition.

It is a short way to write:

```javascript
i = i + 1;
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Try It"}
Change `i < 3` to `i < 5`. Predict how many times the message will appear before you run the code.
:::

## 6.3 Trace a Loop One Step at a Time

Loops become easier when you trace the changing value.

Consider:

```javascript
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  console.log(i);
}
```

JavaScript follows these steps:

| Repetition | Value of `i` | Is `i < 3` true? | What happens? |
|---|---:|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | yes | print `0` |
| 2 | 1 | yes | print `1` |
| 3 | 2 | yes | print `2` |
| stop | 3 | no | leave the loop |

So the output is:

```text
0
1
2
```

Why does it begin with `0` instead of `1`?

Because JavaScript arrays also begin counting positions at `0`. Starting a loop at `0` will soon become very useful.

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch Out: `<` Is Important"}
If the loop starts at `0`, then this repeats **three** times:

```javascript
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++)
```

The values are `0`, `1`, and `2`.

Using `i <= 3` would also include `3`, so the loop would repeat four times.
:::

## 6.4 Arrays Store Several Values Together

In Chapter 3, you learned that a variable can store different kinds of values. An **array** is a value that can hold several items in order.

Suppose our game has three monsters:

```javascript
const monsterIds = ["slime", "bat", "ghost"];
```

The square brackets `[` and `]` create an array.

The array has three items:

```text
Index:       0        1        2
             ↓        ↓        ↓
Value:   "slime"   "bat"   "ghost"
```

We can get one item by putting its index in square brackets:

```javascript
console.log(monsterIds[0]); // slime
console.log(monsterIds[1]); // bat
console.log(monsterIds[2]); // ghost
```

The first item is index `0`, not index `1`.

### Use `.length` to ask how many items are in an array

```javascript
console.log(monsterIds.length);
```

For our array, `monsterIds.length` is `3`.

This is better than writing the number `3` directly in many places. If we add another monster later, the array's length changes automatically.

::: {.callout-note title="Understand"}
For an array with 3 items:

- `.length` is `3`;
- valid indexes are `0`, `1`, and `2`;
- the last index is one less than the length.
:::

## 6.5 Loop Through an Array

Now we can combine a loop with an array.

```javascript
const monsterIds = ["slime", "bat", "ghost"];

for (let i = 0; i < monsterIds.length; i++) {
  console.log(monsterIds[i]);
}
```

Trace it:

```text
i = 0 → monsterIds[0] → "slime"
i = 1 → monsterIds[1] → "bat"
i = 2 → monsterIds[2] → "ghost"
i = 3 → 3 < 3 is false → stop
```

This pattern is extremely useful:

```javascript
for (let i = 0; i < arrayName.length; i++) {
  // use arrayName[i]
}
```

Read it in plain language:

> Start at the first array position. Keep going while the index is smaller than the number of items. Move to the next position each time.

### Why use `.length`?

Suppose we add a fourth monster:

```javascript
const monsterIds = ["slime", "bat", "ghost", "dragon"];
```

Our loop still works:

```javascript
for (let i = 0; i < monsterIds.length; i++) {
  console.log(monsterIds[i]);
}
```

We do not need to change `3` into `4`. The loop asks the array for its current length.

## 6.6 Upgrade the Monster Clicker: One Loop, Many Monsters

Now we can solve the real game problem.

Our HTML contains three monster buttons:

```html
<div id="monsters">
  <button id="slime" class="monster">Slime</button>
  <button id="bat" class="monster">Bat</button>
  <button id="ghost" class="monster">Ghost</button>
</div>
```

The JavaScript stores their IDs in an array:

```javascript
const monsterIds = ["slime", "bat", "ghost"];
```

Then a loop visits each ID:

```javascript
for (let i = 0; i < monsterIds.length; i++) {
  const monster = document.getElementById(monsterIds[i]);
  monster.addEventListener("click", hitMonster);
}
```

Look carefully at the line inside the loop:

```javascript
const monster = document.getElementById(monsterIds[i]);
```

Each time the loop repeats, `monsterIds[i]` is different.

```text
First time:  monsterIds[0] → "slime"
Second time: monsterIds[1] → "bat"
Third time:  monsterIds[2] → "ghost"
```

So the browser finds each monster and connects the same `hitMonster()` function to it.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[monsterIds array] --> B[i = 0: slime]
    B --> C[i = 1: bat]
    C --> D[i = 2: ghost]
    D --> E[All three use hitMonster]
```

This is an important programming skill: **when several objects need the same setup, put their information in a collection and loop through it.**

## 6.7 Keep the Score and Branches from Earlier Chapters

The loop is new, but we do not throw away the code from Chapters 4 and 5.

We still keep the score:

```javascript
let score = 0;
const scoreText = document.getElementById("score");
const message = document.getElementById("message");
```

We still update the score when a monster is clicked:

```javascript
function hitMonster() {
  score = score + 1;
  scoreText.textContent = score;

  if (score < 5) {
    message.textContent = "Keep hunting!";
  } else if (score < 10) {
    message.textContent = "Monster Hunter!";
  } else {
    message.textContent = "Monster Master!";
  }
}
```

And the Power Hit rule still uses a branch:

```javascript
function powerHit() {
  if (score >= 5) {
    score = score - 5;
    scoreText.textContent = score;
    message.textContent = "POWER HIT!";
  } else {
    message.textContent = "You need 5 points for a Power Hit.";
  }
}
```

Notice that branches and loops do different jobs:

| Tool | Question it answers | Monster Clicker example |
|---|---|---|
| `if` / `else` | **Should** this code run? | Is the score at least 5? |
| `for` loop | **How many times** should this code run? | Connect every monster button |

A game often needs both.

## 6.8 Build the Complete Monster Swarm Game

Here is the complete version. It continues the ideas from Chapters 3, 4, and 5, but replaces repeated monster setup with a loop.

[COMPLETE EXAMPLE | `index.html`]{.code-label}

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Monster Swarm</title>
  <style>
    body {
      font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
      text-align: center;
      background: #eef7ff;
      color: #17243b;
    }

    main {
      max-width: 650px;
      margin: 40px auto;
      padding: 24px;
      background: white;
      border: 3px solid #17243b;
      border-radius: 20px;
    }

    #monsters {
      display: flex;
      justify-content: center;
      gap: 12px;
      flex-wrap: wrap;
      margin: 24px 0;
    }

    .monster {
      padding: 18px;
      font-size: 1.1rem;
      border: 2px solid #17243b;
      border-radius: 14px;
      background: #e7dcff;
      cursor: pointer;
    }

    #powerHit {
      padding: 12px 18px;
      font-weight: bold;
      cursor: pointer;
    }

    #message {
      min-height: 1.5em;
      font-weight: bold;
    }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <main>
    <h1>Monster Swarm</h1>
    <p>Score: <span id="score">0</span></p>

    <div id="monsters">
      <button id="slime" class="monster">🟢 Slime</button>
      <button id="bat" class="monster">🦇 Bat</button>
      <button id="ghost" class="monster">👻 Ghost</button>
    </div>

    <button id="powerHit">⚡ Power Hit (-5 points)</button>
    <p id="message">Click any monster to begin!</p>
  </main>

  <script>
    let score = 0;

    const scoreText = document.getElementById("score");
    const message = document.getElementById("message");
    const powerHitButton = document.getElementById("powerHit");

    const monsterIds = ["slime", "bat", "ghost"];

    function updateLevelMessage() {
      if (score < 5) {
        message.textContent = "Keep hunting!";
      } else if (score < 10) {
        message.textContent = "Monster Hunter!";
      } else {
        message.textContent = "Monster Master!";
      }
    }

    function hitMonster() {
      score = score + 1;
      scoreText.textContent = score;
      updateLevelMessage();
    }

    function powerHit() {
      if (score >= 5) {
        score = score - 5;
        scoreText.textContent = score;
        message.textContent = "POWER HIT!";
      } else {
        message.textContent = "You need 5 points for a Power Hit.";
      }
    }

    for (let i = 0; i < monsterIds.length; i++) {
      const monster = document.getElementById(monsterIds[i]);
      monster.addEventListener("click", hitMonster);
    }

    powerHitButton.addEventListener("click", powerHit);
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

### What is new in this version?

The important new code is the array:

```javascript
const monsterIds = ["slime", "bat", "ghost"];
```

and the loop:

```javascript
for (let i = 0; i < monsterIds.length; i++) {
  const monster = document.getElementById(monsterIds[i]);
  monster.addEventListener("click", hitMonster);
}
```

Everything else builds on ideas you already know:

```text
DOM element        → Chapter 4
click event        → Chapter 4
score variable     → Chapter 3
if / else branches → Chapter 5
array + loop       → Chapter 6
```

This is how larger programs grow: keep useful code, then add one new idea that solves the next problem.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try It: Add One More Monster"}
Add this button to the HTML:

```html
<button id="dragon" class="monster">🐉 Dragon</button>
```

Then add only one value to the array:

```javascript
const monsterIds = ["slime", "bat", "ghost", "dragon"];
```

You do **not** need another `addEventListener()` line. The loop takes care of the new monster.
:::

## 6.9 A `while` Loop Repeats While a Condition Is True

A `for` loop is useful when you can count repetitions or move through an array.

JavaScript also has a **`while` loop**:

```javascript
let energy = 3;

while (energy > 0) {
  console.log("Monster attack!");
  energy = energy - 1;
}
```

Read it as:

> While `energy > 0` is true, keep running the block.

The values change like this:

```text
energy = 3 → run
energy = 2 → run
energy = 1 → run
energy = 0 → stop
```

A `while` loop is useful when the stopping rule matters more than a fixed number of repetitions.

For now, use a `for` loop as your main tool for stepping through arrays.

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch Out: Infinite Loops"}
A loop must eventually reach a stopping condition.

This loop never changes `energy`:

```javascript
let energy = 3;

while (energy > 0) {
  console.log("Attack!");
}
```

Because `energy` stays `3`, the condition stays true forever. This is called an **infinite loop**.

When writing a loop, always ask: **What changes so this loop can stop?**
:::

## 6.10 Another Way to Loop Through an Array

Once you are comfortable with the three-part `for` loop, JavaScript has a shorter form for reading every value in an array:

```javascript
const monsterIds = ["slime", "bat", "ghost"];

for (const monsterId of monsterIds) {
  console.log(monsterId);
}
```

This is called a **`for...of` loop**.

Read it as:

> For each `monsterId` of `monsterIds`, run this code.

We could use it in our game:

```javascript
for (const monsterId of monsterIds) {
  const monster = document.getElementById(monsterId);
  monster.addEventListener("click", hitMonster);
}
```

This version is shorter, but the regular `for` loop is still important because it teaches you how a loop starts, tests a condition, changes, and uses array indexes.

::: {.callout-important collapse="true" title="Advanced Study: `for` or `for...of`?"}
Use a regular `for` loop when you need the index number:

```javascript
for (let i = 0; i < monsterIds.length; i++) {
  console.log(i, monsterIds[i]);
}
```

Use `for...of` when you mainly need each value:

```javascript
for (const monsterId of monsterIds) {
  console.log(monsterId);
}
```

Both are useful. The best choice depends on what information your code needs.
:::

# Make Things Change Over Time {#sec-ch07}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[GAME 07 | Catch the Star]{.game-title}

[Timers]{.skill-chip} [Coordinates]{.skill-chip} [CSS]{.skill-chip}

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="Structure → Style → Behavior" icon="false"}

**Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior.**

- **Build the scene structure:** Keep a star inside a game-area container, with score and any countdown outside it.
- **Style the scene:** Size the arena and star and establish the positioned parent and starting offsets.
- **Behavior:** Move the star with clicks and a timer; check score, speed changes, and how the game stops.

Use this plan for the examples and exercises below. Reuse parts that already work; change only what the task needs. After each step, predict one result and check it.

:::


::: {.callout-tip .mission title="Your mission" icon="false"}

By the end of this chapter, you can:

- use CSS position values from JavaScript
- use random coordinates
- use `setInterval` and `clearInterval`

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="The big idea" icon="false"}

A moving game world changes even when the player is not clicking. Timers let JavaScript run an action again and again.

:::

## Move an element

An absolutely positioned element can be moved by changing its left and top CSS properties.

![Game coordinates: x moves right, y moves down.](../figures/chapter_05/browser-coordinates.png){#fig-ch07 fig-alt="A coordinate plane starts at the top left. The x axis increases rightward and y increases downward; the star is at 25,35." width="100%"}

**Read the picture:** Start at the top-left corner. Move 25 units right and 35 units down to reach the star. These are example coordinates, not fixed limits for your game; use the size of your own game area.

```javascript
star.style.left = "120px";
star.style.top = "80px";
```

## Pick a random position

A helper function makes the star jump to a new place.

```javascript
function moveStar() {
  const x = Math.floor(Math.random() * 280);
  const y = Math.floor(Math.random() * 180);
  star.style.left = x + "px";
  star.style.top = y + "px";
}
```

## Repeat an action with a timer

`setInterval` calls a function repeatedly. The number is milliseconds, so 1000 means one second.

```javascript
const timerId = setInterval(moveStar, 1000);

// Later, when the game ends:
clearInterval(timerId);
```

## Build the complete game

Put the pieces together. Type the code yourself if you can; typing helps your brain notice punctuation, spelling, and structure.

[COMPLETE EXAMPLE]{.code-label}

```html
<!doctype html>
<html>
<head>
<style>
  #game { position: relative; width: 340px; height: 240px; border: 2px solid #333; }
  #star { position: absolute; font-size: 36px; cursor: pointer; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Catch the Star</h1>
  <p id="score">Score: 0</p>
  <div id="game"><span id="star">⭐</span></div>
<script>
  let score = 0;
  const star = document.getElementById("star");
  const scoreText = document.getElementById("score");

  function moveStar() {
    const x = Math.floor(Math.random() * 280);
    const y = Math.floor(Math.random() * 180);
    star.style.left = x + "px";
    star.style.top = y + "px";
  }

  star.addEventListener("click", function () {
    score++;
    scoreText.textContent = "Score: " + score;
    moveStar();
  });

  moveStar();
  setInterval(moveStar, 1000);
</script>
</body>
</html>
```

Open `workspace/chapter7-catch-the-star/index.html` to watch the complete example. The star moves once per second, and a click raises the score and moves it immediately. The screenshot pages use known positions and control one timer callback so their states are reproducible.

![Catch the Star in Chrome at score zero, with the star near the upper left of the game area.](../figures/chapter_07/star-start.png){#fig-ch07-star-start fig-alt="The Catch the Star page shows Score: 0 and a yellow star near the upper-left corner of a bordered game area." width="100%"}

![Catch the Star in Chrome after one timer move. The star moves while the score stays zero.](../figures/chapter_07/star-after-timer.png){#fig-ch07-star-timer fig-alt="The same game shows Score: 0 with the yellow star near the middle-right of the game area." width="100%"}

![Catch the Star in Chrome after one click. The score is one and the star moves again.](../figures/chapter_07/star-after-click.png){#fig-ch07-star-click fig-alt="The game shows Score: 1 with the yellow star in a new position inside the game area." width="100%"}

**Read the pictures:** The timer calls `moveStar()` without a player action, changing `left` and `top` while the score remains zero. The click handler also calls `moveStar()`, but first it adds one to `score` and updates the paragraph. The regular page keeps its one-second timer; the demonstration pages control when the callback runs for the screenshots.

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="Advanced Study | CSS positioning and browser coordinates" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL DEEPER DIVE]{.study-badge}

For positioned HTML elements, left controls horizontal position and top controls vertical position. In browser coordinates, (0,0) is normally the top-left of the containing area, x increases to the right, and y increases downward. Element sizes matter when keeping an object inside the game area.

```javascript
star.style.left = x + 'px';
star.style.top = y + 'px';
```

**Which box do the coordinates belong to?** `#game { position: relative; }` makes the game area the containing block for the absolutely positioned star. Its offsets are measured from that area, not automatically from the entire page.

**Keep the whole object inside.** The largest useful x offset is approximately the game width minus the star width. The same idea applies to height.

**One timer is enough.** Keep the ID returned by `setInterval()` when you need to stop or replace it. Clearing a timer stops scheduled moves, not the separate click listener.

:::

# Draw Your Own Game World {#sec-ch08}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[GAME 08 | Bouncing Ball]{.game-title}

[Canvas]{.skill-chip} [Animation]{.skill-chip} [Velocity]{.skill-chip}

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="Structure → Style → Behavior" icon="false"}

**Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior.**

- **Build the scene structure:** Create the canvas and list each ball with position, radius, and velocity.
- **Style the scene:** Choose the canvas frame and the ball drawing colors and sizes.
- **Behavior:** Update positions, handle edges, and redraw in one animation loop.

Use this plan for the examples and exercises below. Reuse parts that already work; change only what the task needs. After each step, predict one result and check it.

:::


::: {.callout-tip .mission title="Your mission" icon="false"}

By the end of this chapter, you can:

- create a canvas
- draw shapes with a 2D context
- animate with `requestAnimationFrame`

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="The big idea" icon="false"}

Canvas is different from ordinary HTML. Instead of moving page elements, your code redraws the game world frame after frame.

:::

## Meet canvas

The canvas element is a rectangular drawing surface. JavaScript asks it for a 2D drawing context.

![The animation/game loop repeats update and draw work.](../figures/chapter_06/animation-loop.png){#fig-ch08 fig-alt="A cycle connects read input, update state, draw, and next frame." width="100%"}

**Read the picture:** Each frame is one trip around the cycle. Bouncing Ball has no keyboard input yet, so it begins by updating position. The next chapter adds player input before movement.

```javascript
const canvas = document.getElementById("game");
const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");
```

## Draw a ball

A circle is an arc that goes all the way around.

```javascript
ctx.beginPath();
ctx.arc(x, y, 15, 0, Math.PI * 2);
ctx.fill();
```

## Animation is update + draw + repeat

Each frame changes the position, clears the old picture, draws the new picture, and asks the browser for another frame.

```javascript
function loop() {
  x = x + dx;
  y = y + dy;

  ctx.clearRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
  drawBall();

  requestAnimationFrame(loop);
}
```

## Bounce at the edges

Reverse a velocity when the ball reaches a wall.

```javascript
if (x < radius || x > canvas.width - radius) {
  dx = -dx;
}
if (y < radius || y > canvas.height - radius) {
  dy = -dy;
}
```

## Build the complete game

Put the pieces together. Type the code yourself if you can; typing helps your brain notice punctuation, spelling, and structure.

[COMPLETE EXAMPLE]{.code-label}

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Bouncing Ball</title>
  <style>
    body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; color: #17243b; }
    canvas { border: 2px solid #17243b; background: #f0f7ff; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Bouncing Ball</h1>
  <canvas id="game" width="500" height="300"></canvas>
  <script>
    const canvas = document.getElementById("game");
    const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");
    let x = 100, y = 80;
    let dx = 3, dy = 2;
    const radius = 15;

    function drawBall() {
      ctx.beginPath();
      ctx.arc(x, y, radius, 0, Math.PI * 2);
      ctx.fillStyle = "#6d3df5";
      ctx.fill();
    }

    function loop() {
      x += dx;
      y += dy;
      if (x < radius || x > canvas.width - radius) dx = -dx;
      if (y < radius || y > canvas.height - radius) dy = -dy;
      ctx.clearRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
      drawBall();
      requestAnimationFrame(loop);
    }
    loop();
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

Open `workspace/chapter6-bouncing-ball/index.html` to watch the complete example. The browser redraws the purple ball on every animation frame. The screenshot pages pause automatic frames and call the same `loop()` function a known number of times.

![Bouncing Ball in Chrome near its starting position inside the canvas.](../figures/chapter_06/ball-start.png){#fig-ch08-ball-start fig-alt="A purple ball appears near the upper-left of a light blue bordered canvas." width="100%"}

![Bouncing Ball in Chrome after twenty more animation frames. The ball has moved right and down.](../figures/chapter_06/ball-after-frames.png){#fig-ch08-ball-frames fig-alt="The purple ball is farther right and lower in the same canvas." width="100%"}

![Bouncing Ball in Chrome after reaching the right wall and reversing horizontal direction.](../figures/chapter_06/ball-bounce.png){#fig-ch08-ball-bounce fig-alt="The purple ball is next to the right edge of the canvas." width="100%"}

**Read the pictures:** Every `loop()` call changes `x` and `y`, clears the previous drawing, and draws the ball again. At the right wall, `dx` becomes negative, so the next frames move left. The regular page uses `requestAnimationFrame()` to continue automatically.

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="Advanced Study | requestAnimationFrame and frame time" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL DEEPER DIVE]{.study-badge}

`requestAnimationFrame` asks the browser to run your animation code before the next repaint. Real games should not assume every computer draws the same number of frames per second. Advanced games use the timestamp passed to the callback to calculate delta time so motion depends on elapsed time, not frame count.

```javascript
let previousTime;
function loop(time) {
  const dt = previousTime === undefined
    ? 0
    : (time - previousTime) / 1000;
  previousTime = time;
  update(dt); // Speeds are in pixels per second.
  draw();
  requestAnimationFrame(loop);
}
requestAnimationFrame(loop);
```

**The timestamp is not the time since the last frame.** Subtract the previous timestamp and divide milliseconds by 1000 to get seconds. A speed of 180 pixels per second moves about 3 pixels in a 1/60-second frame.

This is a timing pattern, not a second loop to add beside the existing one. Supply your own `update(dt)` and `draw()` functions. Start the pattern with `requestAnimationFrame(loop)`. A more robust game should also handle a long pause, for example by resetting its previous timestamp when resuming.

Further reading: [MDN: requestAnimationFrame](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/requestAnimationFrame).

:::

# Control a Real-Time Game {#sec-ch09}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[GAME 09 | Pong]{.game-title}

[Keyboard input]{.skill-chip} [State]{.skill-chip} [Collision]{.skill-chip}

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="Structure → Style → Behavior" icon="false"}

**Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior.**

- **Build the scene structure:** Place the canvas, paddles, ball, instructions, and score display.
- **Style the scene:** Draw distinguishable paddles and ball and make the controls and score legible.
- **Behavior:** Read held keys, update movement, resolve paddle hits, and test scoring and misses.

Use this plan for the examples and exercises below. Reuse parts that already work; change only what the task needs. After each step, predict one result and check it.

:::


::: {.callout-note .code-guide title="How to use the code pieces" icon="false"}

The short snippets below explain individual rules. The complete browser example later in this chapter combines them into a playable page.

:::

::: {.callout-tip .mission title="Your mission" icon="false"}

By the end of this chapter, you can:

- track pressed keys
- move a paddle every frame
- detect simple rectangle/ball collisions

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="The big idea" icon="false"}

In a real-time game, a key press should change what happens during the next frames. Instead of moving once per key event, we remember which keys are held down.

:::

## Remember key state

`keydown` sets a state to `true`. `keyup` changes it back to `false`.

![Keyboard events update state; the game loop uses that state.](../figures/chapter_07/keyboard-state.png){#fig-ch09 fig-alt="Keydown sets a pressed flag to true, keyup sets it to false, and the game loop uses the flag." width="100%"}

**Read the picture:** An event changes a remembered value. The loop can then read that value on many frames. The picture uses a right-arrow flag; Pong uses the same idea for the up and down arrows.

```javascript
const keys = {};

window.addEventListener("keydown", e => {
  keys[e.key] = true;
});
window.addEventListener("keyup", e => {
  keys[e.key] = false;
});
```

## Move during the update

The game loop checks the state every frame.

```javascript
if (keys["ArrowUp"]) paddleY -= 5;
if (keys["ArrowDown"]) paddleY += 5;
```

## Keep the paddle on the screen

`Math.max` and `Math.min` can clamp a value inside a range.

```javascript
paddleY = Math.max(0, paddleY);
paddleY = Math.min(canvas.height - paddleH, paddleY);
```

## Paddle collision idea

For a first Pong game, place a vertical paddle on the right. Here, paddleX and paddleY are its top-left coordinates, paddleW and paddleH are its size, and positive dx means the ball is moving right. Test the ball bounding box against the paddle before reversing direction.

```javascript
const overlapsPaddle = (
  ballX + radius >= paddleX &&
  ballX - radius <= paddleX + paddleW &&
  ballY + radius >= paddleY &&
  ballY - radius <= paddleY + paddleH
);
if (dx > 0 && overlapsPaddle) {
  ballX = paddleX - radius;
  dx = -Math.abs(dx);
}
```

## Play Pong in your browser {.unnumbered}

Save this page as `index.html`, or open `workspace/chapter9-pong/index.html`. Hold the up or down arrow to move the right paddle. The game loop reads the remembered key state every frame and checks whether the ball overlaps the paddle.

[COMPLETE EXAMPLE | `index.html`]{.code-label}

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Pong Practice</title>
  <style>
    body { margin: 0; min-height: 100vh; display: grid; place-items: center; background: #eaf4ff; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; color: #17243b; }
    main { padding: 24px; border: 3px solid #17243b; border-radius: 18px; background: white; }
    h1 { margin: 0 0 8px; color: #5d35d5; }
    canvas { display: block; border: 2px solid #17243b; background: #102342; }
    #status { min-height: 1.5em; margin-bottom: 0; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <main>
    <h1>Pong Practice</h1>
    <p>Hold ↑ or ↓ to move the paddle.</p>
    <canvas id="game" width="560" height="320"></canvas>
    <p id="status">Paddle hits: 0</p>
  </main>
  <script>
    const canvas = document.getElementById("game");
    const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");
    const status = document.getElementById("status");
    const keys = {};
    window.addEventListener("keydown", e => {
      if (e.key === "ArrowUp" || e.key === "ArrowDown") e.preventDefault();
      keys[e.key] = true;
    });
    window.addEventListener("keyup", e => { keys[e.key] = false; });
    window.addEventListener("blur", () => {
      keys.ArrowUp = false;
      keys.ArrowDown = false;
    });

    const paddleX = 530, paddleW = 12, paddleH = 70;
    let paddleY = 125;
    let ballX = 100, ballY = 160;
    let dx = 3, dy = 2;
    const radius = 10;
    let hits = 0;

    function update() {
      if (keys["ArrowUp"]) paddleY -= 5;
      if (keys["ArrowDown"]) paddleY += 5;
      paddleY = Math.max(0, paddleY);
      paddleY = Math.min(canvas.height - paddleH, paddleY);

      ballX += dx;
      ballY += dy;
      if (ballX < radius) dx = Math.abs(dx);
      if (ballY < radius || ballY > canvas.height - radius) dy = -dy;

      const overlapsPaddle = (
        ballX + radius >= paddleX &&
        ballX - radius <= paddleX + paddleW &&
        ballY + radius >= paddleY &&
        ballY - radius <= paddleY + paddleH
      );
      if (dx > 0 && overlapsPaddle) {
        ballX = paddleX - radius;
        dx = -Math.abs(dx);
        hits++;
        status.textContent = "Paddle hits: " + hits;
      }
      if (ballX > canvas.width + radius) {
        ballX = 100;
        ballY = canvas.height / 2;
        dx = Math.abs(dx);
        status.textContent = "Missed! Paddle hits: " + hits;
      }
    }

    function draw() {
      ctx.clearRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
      ctx.fillStyle = "#102342";
      ctx.fillRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
      ctx.fillStyle = "#86d8ff";
      ctx.fillRect(paddleX, paddleY, paddleW, paddleH);
      ctx.beginPath();
      ctx.arc(ballX, ballY, radius, 0, Math.PI * 2);
      ctx.fillStyle = "#ffe48a";
      ctx.fill();
    }

    function loop() {
      update();
      draw();
      requestAnimationFrame(loop);
    }
    draw();
    requestAnimationFrame(loop);
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

The demonstration pages pause automatic animation, then make a known number of updates or one paddle collision. The playable page keeps animating normally.

![Pong Practice in Chrome before the paddle moves.](../figures/chapter_09/pong-start.png){#fig-ch09-pong-start fig-alt="A dark Pong canvas shows a yellow ball, a blue paddle on the right, and Paddle hits: 0." width="100%"}
![Pong Practice in Chrome after holding the up arrow for twelve updates.](../figures/chapter_09/pong-paddle-up.png){#fig-ch09-pong-up fig-alt="The blue paddle has moved upward after held-key updates while the ball moves across the canvas." width="100%"}
![Pong Practice in Chrome after a ball and paddle collision.](../figures/chapter_09/pong-paddle-hit.png){#fig-ch09-pong-hit fig-alt="The yellow ball touches the right paddle and the page says Paddle hits: 1." width="100%"}

**Read the pictures:** A held key keeps `keys["ArrowUp"]` true, so the paddle moves through several updates. When the ball reaches the paddle, the overlap test becomes true and `dx` changes sign. The hit count confirms that the collision response ran once.

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="Advanced Study | Input state versus input events" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL DEEPER DIVE]{.study-badge}

An event tells you that something happened once. A state variable remembers whether a key is currently held down. Real-time games usually update state in `keydown`/`keyup` handlers and let the game loop decide how far to move the player each frame.

```javascript
let rightPressed = false;
window.addEventListener("keydown", e => {
  if (e.key === "ArrowRight") rightPressed = true;
});
window.addEventListener("keyup", e => {
  if (e.key === "ArrowRight") rightPressed = false;
});
```

**Events are messages; state is memory.** Holding a key may produce repeated `keydown` events, but we do not use those repeats as a movement clock. A true flag means the loop should keep moving the paddle.

**Focus matters.** A finished game should clear remembered keys when it loses focus, because a key-up event may not arrive where expected. Prevent arrow-key scrolling only while the player is controlling the game, rather than blocking page navigation everywhere.

:::

# Manage Many Game Objects {#sec-ch10}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[GAME 10 | Breakout]{.game-title}

[Objects]{.skill-chip} [Arrays]{.skill-chip} [Loops]{.skill-chip}

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="Structure → Style → Behavior" icon="false"}

**Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior.**

- **Build the scene structure:** Describe the paddle, ball, and brick collection, including positions and active flags.
- **Style the scene:** Draw the bricks and any remaining-hit feedback so their state is visible.
- **Behavior:** Process the collection, handle each hit once, and check score and victory rules.

Use this plan for the examples and exercises below. Reuse parts that already work; change only what the task needs. After each step, predict one result and check it.

:::


::: {.callout-note .code-guide title="How to use the code pieces" icon="false"}

The short snippets below explain individual rules. The complete browser example later in this chapter combines them into a playable page.

:::

::: {.callout-tip .mission title="Your mission" icon="false"}

By the end of this chapter, you can:

- store many objects in an array
- use loops to update and draw objects
- remove or mark hit bricks
- understand basic collision tests

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="The big idea" icon="false"}

Breakout has many bricks. We do not want 30 separate variables. Arrays let one variable hold a whole collection of game objects.

:::

## Store bricks as objects

Each brick can be an object with position, size, and whether it is still active.

![Collision detection asks whether game objects overlap.](../figures/chapter_08/collision-overlap.png){#fig-ch10 fig-alt="Two rectangles partially overlap; the shared area illustrates a rectangular collision test." width="100%"}

**Read the picture:** A collision is not just being close. The shapes overlap horizontally **and** vertically. The picture uses rectangles; the beginner ball test uses a square bounding box around the ball.

```javascript
const bricks = [
  { x: 20, y: 20, w: 60, h: 20, alive: true },
  { x: 90, y: 20, w: 60, h: 20, alive: true },
  { x: 160, y: 20, w: 60, h: 20, alive: true }
];
```

## Loop through the array

`for...of` gives us each brick one at a time.

```javascript
for (const brick of bricks) {
  if (brick.alive) {
    ctx.fillRect(brick.x, brick.y, brick.w, brick.h);
  }
}
```

## A simple collision test

A ball hits a brick when its position overlaps the brick rectangle. For a beginner version, we can use the ball center plus its radius.

```javascript
function hitsBrick(ballX, ballY, r, brick) {
  return (
    ballX + r > brick.x &&
    ballX - r < brick.x + brick.w &&
    ballY + r > brick.y &&
    ballY - r < brick.y + brick.h
  );
}
```

## Change the world after a hit

When a collision happens, mark the brick as no longer alive and reverse the vertical direction of the ball.

```javascript
if (brick.alive && hitsBrick(x, y, radius, brick)) {
  brick.alive = false;
  dy = -dy;
  score++;
}
```

## Play Breakout in your browser {.unnumbered}

Save this page as `index.html`, or open `workspace/chapter10-breakout/index.html`. Each brick is an object in the `bricks` array. The loop draws only active bricks and tests the ball against them.

[COMPLETE EXAMPLE | `index.html`]{.code-label}

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Breakout Practice</title>
  <style>
    body { margin: 0; min-height: 100vh; display: grid; place-items: center; background: #fff3e8; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; color: #17243b; }
    main { padding: 24px; border: 3px solid #17243b; border-radius: 18px; background: white; }
    h1 { margin: 0 0 8px; color: #c04a5a; }
    canvas { display: block; border: 2px solid #17243b; background: #17243b; }
    #status { min-height: 1.5em; margin-bottom: 0; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <main>
    <h1>Breakout Practice</h1>
    <p>Hold ← or → to move the paddle and catch the ball.</p>
    <canvas id="game" width="560" height="360"></canvas>
    <p id="status">Bricks cleared: 0</p>
  </main>
  <script>
    const canvas = document.getElementById("game");
    const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");
    const status = document.getElementById("status");
    const keys = {};
    window.addEventListener("keydown", e => {
      if (e.key === "ArrowLeft" || e.key === "ArrowRight") e.preventDefault();
      keys[e.key] = true;
    });
    window.addEventListener("keyup", e => { keys[e.key] = false; });
    window.addEventListener("blur", () => {
      keys.ArrowLeft = false;
      keys.ArrowRight = false;
    });

    const bricks = [
      { x: 45, y: 40, w: 100, h: 22, alive: true },
      { x: 165, y: 40, w: 100, h: 22, alive: true },
      { x: 285, y: 40, w: 100, h: 22, alive: true },
      { x: 405, y: 40, w: 100, h: 22, alive: true },
      { x: 45, y: 76, w: 100, h: 22, alive: true },
      { x: 165, y: 76, w: 100, h: 22, alive: true },
      { x: 285, y: 76, w: 100, h: 22, alive: true },
      { x: 405, y: 76, w: 100, h: 22, alive: true }
    ];
    let paddleX = 230;
    const paddleY = 330, paddleW = 100, paddleH = 12;
    let x = 280, y = 250, dx = 3, dy = -3;
    const radius = 10;
    let score = 0;

    function hitsBrick(ballX, ballY, r, brick) {
      return (
        ballX + r > brick.x &&
        ballX - r < brick.x + brick.w &&
        ballY + r > brick.y &&
        ballY - r < brick.y + brick.h
      );
    }

    function update() {
      if (keys.ArrowLeft) paddleX -= 6;
      if (keys.ArrowRight) paddleX += 6;
      paddleX = Math.max(0, Math.min(canvas.width - paddleW, paddleX));
      x += dx;
      y += dy;
      if (x < radius || x > canvas.width - radius) dx = -dx;
      if (y < radius) dy = Math.abs(dy);
      if (dy > 0 && y + radius >= paddleY && y - radius <= paddleY + paddleH &&
          x + radius >= paddleX && x - radius <= paddleX + paddleW) {
        y = paddleY - radius;
        dy = -Math.abs(dy);
      }
      for (const brick of bricks) {
        if (brick.alive && hitsBrick(x, y, radius, brick)) {
          brick.alive = false;
          dy = -dy;
          score++;
          status.textContent = "Bricks cleared: " + score;
          break;
        }
      }
      if (y > canvas.height + radius) {
        x = canvas.width / 2;
        y = 250;
        dy = -3;
        status.textContent = "Try again! Bricks cleared: " + score;
      }
    }

    function draw() {
      ctx.clearRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
      ctx.fillStyle = "#17243b";
      ctx.fillRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
      for (const brick of bricks) {
        if (brick.alive) {
          ctx.fillStyle = brick.y === 40 ? "#f899b5" : "#ffe48a";
          ctx.fillRect(brick.x, brick.y, brick.w, brick.h);
        }
      }
      ctx.fillStyle = "#8ce3ff";
      ctx.fillRect(paddleX, paddleY, paddleW, paddleH);
      ctx.beginPath();
      ctx.arc(x, y, radius, 0, Math.PI * 2);
      ctx.fillStyle = "white";
      ctx.fill();
    }

    function loop() {
      update();
      draw();
      requestAnimationFrame(loop);
    }
    draw();
    requestAnimationFrame(loop);
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

The demonstration pages pause automatic animation and place the ball for one or three known brick collisions. The playable page keeps animating normally.

![Breakout Practice in Chrome before a brick is hit.](../figures/chapter_10/breakout-start.png){#fig-ch10-breakout-start fig-alt="A Breakout canvas shows eight colored bricks, a ball, a paddle, and Bricks cleared: 0." width="100%"}
![Breakout Practice in Chrome after one brick collision.](../figures/chapter_10/breakout-one-hit.png){#fig-ch10-breakout-one fig-alt="One top-row brick is missing and the page says Bricks cleared: 1." width="100%"}
![Breakout Practice in Chrome after three brick collisions.](../figures/chapter_10/breakout-three-hits.png){#fig-ch10-breakout-three fig-alt="Three top-row bricks are missing and the page says Bricks cleared: 3." width="100%"}

**Read the pictures:** `hitsBrick()` finds an overlap, then the code sets that brick's `alive` property to false. The next draw skips it, so a gap appears in the row. The score rises from zero to one, then three. The brick object stays in the array even though it is no longer drawn or hit.

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="Advanced Study | Objects, arrays, and collision logic" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL DEEPER DIVE]{.study-badge}

An object groups properties that belong to one game object. An array stores many objects in order. A common rectangle collision test checks whether one rectangle is not completely left, right, above, or below the other. Larger games often separate `update()`, `draw()`, and collision functions.

```javascript
const brick = { x: 40, y: 20, w: 60, h: 20, alive: true };
bricks.push(brick);
```

**Each object is one brick; the array is the collection.** `brick.alive = false` changes a property on that brick. A `for...of` loop can visit the collection when checking collisions and when drawing.

**Know the approximation.** `hitsBrick` checks the square around the ball against the brick. At a corner, those squares can overlap before the circle itself touches. A fast ball can also jump past a thin brick between frames.

**One hit, one response.** Avoid reversing the ball repeatedly for several bricks in one update. A simple first approach is to stop checking after the first detected hit.

:::

# Build a World on a Grid {#sec-ch11}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[GAME 11 | Snake]{.game-title}

[Grid cells]{.skill-chip} [Arrays]{.skill-chip} [Game state]{.skill-chip}

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="Structure → Style → Behavior" icon="false"}

**Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior.**

- **Build the scene structure:** Describe the grid, snake cells, food, obstacles, and start/restart controls.
- **Style the scene:** Make food, snake, walls, and game-state messages visually distinct.
- **Behavior:** Update grid movement, growth, collisions, speed changes, and resets.

Use this plan for the examples and exercises below. Reuse parts that already work; change only what the task needs. After each step, predict one result and check it.

:::


::: {.callout-note .code-guide title="How to use the code pieces" icon="false"}

The short snippets below explain individual rules. The complete browser example later in this chapter combines them into a playable page.

:::

::: {.callout-tip .mission title="Your mission" icon="false"}

By the end of this chapter, you can:

- represent positions as grid cells
- store the snake as an array
- update the world one step at a time
- detect self and wall collisions

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="The big idea" icon="false"}

Snake becomes easier when the world is a grid. Instead of moving by tiny pixels, the snake moves one cell at a time.

:::

## A snake is a list of body cells

The first item can be the head. Each cell stores x and y coordinates.

![A grid game stores positions as x/y cells.](../figures/chapter_09/snake-grid.png){#fig-ch11 fig-alt="A snake occupies three adjacent cells in a grid. A food cell is above and to the right of the head." width="100%"}

**Read the picture:** Each square is one cell, not one screen pixel. The head is the first item in the body array. The arrow points toward food; it does not allow a diagonal move. Move one horizontal or vertical cell per step.

```javascript
let snake = [
  { x: 5, y: 5 },
  { x: 4, y: 5 },
  { x: 3, y: 5 }
];
```

## Move by creating a new head

We calculate a new head from the old head and the current direction. Then `unshift` adds it to the front. `pop` removes the last tail cell.

```javascript
const head = snake[0];
const newHead = { x: head.x + dx, y: head.y + dy };
snake.unshift(newHead);
snake.pop();
```

## Grow when food is eaten

If the head lands on food, do not remove the tail that step. The snake becomes one cell longer.

```javascript
if (newHead.x === food.x && newHead.y === food.y) {
  score++;
  placeFood();
} else {
  snake.pop();
}
```

## Prevent instant reverse direction

If the snake is moving right, switching directly to left would make the head collide with the body. Check the old direction before accepting the new one.

```javascript
if (e.key === "ArrowLeft" && dx !== 1) {
  dx = -1;
  dy = 0;
}
```

## Play Snake in your browser {.unnumbered}

Save this page as `index.html`, or open `workspace/chapter9-snake/index.html`. The snake is an array of grid cells. Each step adds a new head; eating food keeps the tail, and an ordinary step removes it.

[COMPLETE EXAMPLE | `index.html`]{.code-label}

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Snake Grid</title>
  <style>
    body { margin: 0; min-height: 100vh; display: grid; place-items: center; background: #e8f8ef; color: #193b2d; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
    main { padding: 24px; border: 3px solid #193b2d; border-radius: 18px; background: white; }
    h1 { margin: 0 0 8px; color: #24875d; }
    canvas { display: block; border: 2px solid #193b2d; background: #f4fff8; }
    button { margin-top: 10px; padding: 8px 14px; font: inherit; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <main>
    <h1>Snake Grid</h1>
    <p>Use arrow keys. Eat the red food; avoid walls and your body.</p>
    <canvas id="game" width="400" height="400"></canvas>
    <p id="status">Score: 0</p>
    <button id="restart" type="button">Restart</button>
  </main>
  <script>
    const canvas = document.getElementById("game");
    const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");
    const status = document.getElementById("status");
    const cell = 20, count = canvas.width / cell;
    let snake, food, dx, dy, score, gameOver, turned;

    function reset() {
      snake = [{ x: 5, y: 5 }, { x: 4, y: 5 }, { x: 3, y: 5 }];
      food = { x: 8, y: 5 };
      dx = 1; dy = 0; score = 0; gameOver = false; turned = false;
      status.textContent = "Score: 0";
      draw();
    }

    function placeFood() {
      do {
        food = { x: Math.floor(Math.random() * count), y: Math.floor(Math.random() * count) };
      } while (snake.some(part => part.x === food.x && part.y === food.y));
    }

    window.addEventListener("keydown", e => {
      const turns = { ArrowUp: [0, -1], ArrowDown: [0, 1], ArrowLeft: [-1, 0], ArrowRight: [1, 0] };
      const next = turns[e.key];
      if (!next) return;
      e.preventDefault();
      if (!turned && (next[0] !== -dx || next[1] !== -dy)) {
        [dx, dy] = next;
        turned = true;
      }
    });
    document.getElementById("restart").addEventListener("click", reset);

    function step() {
      if (gameOver) return;
      const head = snake[0];
      const newHead = { x: head.x + dx, y: head.y + dy };
      const eating = newHead.x === food.x && newHead.y === food.y;
      const body = eating ? snake : snake.slice(0, -1);
      if (newHead.x < 0 || newHead.x >= count || newHead.y < 0 || newHead.y >= count ||
          body.some(part => part.x === newHead.x && part.y === newHead.y)) {
        gameOver = true;
        status.textContent = "Game over! Score: " + score + ". Press Restart.";
        draw();
        return;
      }
      snake.unshift(newHead);
      if (eating) {
        score++;
        placeFood();
      } else {
        snake.pop();
      }
      turned = false;
      status.textContent = "Score: " + score;
      draw();
    }

    function draw() {
      ctx.fillStyle = "#f4fff8";
      ctx.fillRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
      ctx.strokeStyle = "#d8eedd";
      for (let line = 0; line <= count; line++) {
        ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(line * cell, 0); ctx.lineTo(line * cell, canvas.height); ctx.stroke();
        ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(0, line * cell); ctx.lineTo(canvas.width, line * cell); ctx.stroke();
      }
      ctx.fillStyle = "#e75454";
      ctx.fillRect(food.x * cell + 2, food.y * cell + 2, cell - 4, cell - 4);
      for (const [index, part] of snake.entries()) {
        ctx.fillStyle = index === 0 ? "#176b49" : "#42ae76";
        ctx.fillRect(part.x * cell + 1, part.y * cell + 1, cell - 2, cell - 2);
      }
    }

    reset();
    setInterval(step, 150);
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

The demonstration pages pause the timer and make known steps. The playable page advances every 150 milliseconds.

![Snake Grid in Chrome before the snake reaches the food.](../figures/chapter_09/snake-start.png){#fig-ch11-snake-start fig-alt="A three-cell green snake faces red food on a square grid, with Score: 0." width="100%"}
![Snake Grid in Chrome after the head reaches food and the snake grows.](../figures/chapter_09/snake-food.png){#fig-ch11-snake-food fig-alt="The green snake is four cells long and the page shows Score: 1." width="100%"}
![Snake Grid in Chrome after a wall collision ends the game.](../figures/chapter_09/snake-wall.png){#fig-ch11-snake-wall fig-alt="The snake has reached the right wall and the page says Game over! Score: 0. Press Restart." width="100%"}

**Read the pictures:** The snake starts with three cells. Reaching food raises the score and leaves the tail in place, so it grows to four cells. A move beyond the right edge ends the game. Restart resets the body, direction, food, and score.

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="Advanced Study | Game state as data" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL DEEPER DIVE]{.study-badge}

Snake works well because the entire game can be described as data: an array of body cells, a direction, food coordinates, and score. Separating state from drawing makes the program easier to reason about. The screen becomes a picture of the current state rather than the place where the state is stored.

```javascript
const snake = [
  {x: 3, y: 2},
  {x: 2, y: 2}
];
```

**Grid coordinates are data, not pixels.** At 20 pixels per cell, `{ x: 3, y: 2 }` is drawn with its top-left corner at pixel `(60, 40)`. Multiplication happens during drawing; positions stay stored as cells.

**Choose one tail rule.** Section 9.2 shows constant-length movement. When adding Section 9.3, replace the unconditional `snake.pop()` with the conditional version. Keeping both removes the tail twice on an ordinary step.

**Accept one turn per step.** For a more robust game, allow at most one queued turn between updates, so two fast key presses cannot cause an accidental reversal. Food placement should avoid occupied cells.

:::

# Game Studio {#sec-ch12}

::: {.chapter-banner}

[GAME 12 | Design Your Own Game]{.game-title}

[Design]{.skill-chip} [Playtesting]{.skill-chip} [Modules]{.skill-chip}

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="Structure → Style → Behavior" icon="false"}

**Build the scene structure → Style the scene → Program game behavior.**

- **Build the scene structure:** Sketch the play area and controls; list the player, objects, goal, and state.
- **Style the scene:** Use readable labels and simple distinguishable shapes for a first playable version.
- **Behavior:** Implement one core action, win/lose rules, and restart, then playtest and repeat the flow.

Use this plan for the examples and exercises below. Reuse parts that already work; change only what the task needs. After each step, predict one result and check it.

:::


::: {.callout-note .code-guide title="Your own project" icon="false"}

The planning snippets name jobs a game needs. The complete Catch the Fruit example later in this chapter implements those jobs in one playable page.

:::

::: {.callout-tip .mission title="Your mission" icon="false"}

By the end of this chapter, you can:

- turn an idea into game rules
- plan game state before coding
- build a minimum playable version
- test and improve with player feedback

:::

::: {.callout-note .big-idea title="The big idea" icon="false"}

Game development is not “write all the code and hope.” Good game designers make a tiny playable version, test it, and improve one rule at a time.

:::

## Start with one sentence

Describe the game without features: “The player moves a basket to catch falling fruit.” If the sentence is confusing, the first version of the game is probably too complicated.

## Identify the game state

List the information the program must remember.

```javascript
// Example: Catch the Fruit
let score = 0;
let lives = 3;
let basketX = 200;
let fruitX = 100;
let fruitY = 0;
let gameOver = false;
```

## Write the game loop as a plan

Before writing details, describe the repeating cycle.

```javascript
function loop() {
  updatePlayer();
  updateFruit();
  checkCollisions();
  draw();
  requestAnimationFrame(loop);
}
```

## Build the minimum playable version

Your first version needs only enough features to answer: “Can someone play this?” Leave menus, sound, special powers, and artwork until the core rule works.

::: {.callout-tip .checklist title="Minimum playable version" icon="false"}

- [ ] Player can control something.
- [ ] Something changes over time.
- [ ] There is a clear goal.
- [ ] Success or failure can happen.
- [ ] The game can restart.

:::

## Playtest like a scientist

Give the game to another person without explaining every rule. Watch where they get confused. Ask what they expected to happen. Change one thing and test again.

## Try a minimum playable game {.unnumbered}

The planning sketch becomes **Catch the Fruit** in this complete page. Save it as `index.html`, or open `workspace/chapter10-catch-fruit/index.html`. Move the basket with arrow keys; catch five fruit to win, or lose after three misses.

[COMPLETE EXAMPLE | `index.html`]{.code-label}

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Catch the Fruit</title>
  <style>
    body { margin: 0; min-height: 100vh; display: grid; place-items: center; background: #fff2e4; color: #46301c; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
    main { padding: 24px; border: 3px solid #46301c; border-radius: 18px; background: white; }
    h1 { margin: 0 0 8px; color: #c35a24; }
    canvas { display: block; border: 2px solid #46301c; background: #fffaf2; }
    button { padding: 8px 14px; font: inherit; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <main>
    <h1>Catch the Fruit</h1>
    <p>Move with ← and →. Catch five fruit before losing three lives.</p>
    <canvas id="game" width="500" height="350"></canvas>
    <p id="status">Score: 0 | Lives: 3</p>
    <button id="restart" type="button">Restart</button>
  </main>
  <script>
    const canvas = document.getElementById("game");
    const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");
    const status = document.getElementById("status");
    const keys = {};
    let score = 0;
    let lives = 3;
    let basketX = 200;
    let fruitX = 100;
    let fruitY = 0;
    let gameOver = false;
    const basketY = 310, basketW = 100, basketH = 16, fruitR = 12;

    window.addEventListener("keydown", e => {
      if (e.key === "ArrowLeft" || e.key === "ArrowRight") {
        e.preventDefault();
        keys[e.key] = true;
      }
    });
    window.addEventListener("keyup", e => { keys[e.key] = false; });
    window.addEventListener("blur", () => { keys.ArrowLeft = false; keys.ArrowRight = false; });

    function updatePlayer() {
      if (keys.ArrowLeft) basketX -= 5;
      if (keys.ArrowRight) basketX += 5;
      basketX = Math.max(0, Math.min(canvas.width - basketW, basketX));
    }
    function updateFruit() { fruitY += 3; }
    function checkCollisions() {
      if (fruitY + fruitR < basketY) return;
      const caught = fruitX + fruitR >= basketX && fruitX - fruitR <= basketX + basketW;
      if (caught) score++;
      else lives--;
      fruitX = 25 + Math.floor(Math.random() * (canvas.width - 50));
      fruitY = 0;
      if (score >= 5 || lives <= 0) gameOver = true;
      status.textContent = gameOver
        ? (score >= 5 ? "You win!" : "Game over!") + " Score: " + score + " | Lives: " + lives
        : "Score: " + score + " | Lives: " + lives;
    }
    function draw() {
      ctx.clearRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
      ctx.fillStyle = "#fffaf2";
      ctx.fillRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
      ctx.fillStyle = "#96552d";
      ctx.fillRect(basketX, basketY, basketW, basketH);
      ctx.beginPath();
      ctx.arc(fruitX, fruitY, fruitR, 0, Math.PI * 2);
      ctx.fillStyle = "#e75454";
      ctx.fill();
    }
    function loop() {
      if (gameOver) return;
      updatePlayer();
      updateFruit();
      checkCollisions();
      draw();
      if (!gameOver) requestAnimationFrame(loop);
    }
    function restart() {
      score = 0; lives = 3; basketX = 200; fruitX = 100; fruitY = 0; gameOver = false;
      status.textContent = "Score: 0 | Lives: 3";
      draw();
      requestAnimationFrame(loop);
    }
    document.getElementById("restart").addEventListener("click", restart);
    restart();
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

The screenshot demonstration pages pause automatic frames and arrange one catch or three misses. The playable page uses `requestAnimationFrame()`.

![Catch the Fruit in Chrome at the beginning of a game.](../figures/chapter_10/fruit-start.png){#fig-ch12-fruit-start fig-alt="Catch the Fruit shows a falling red fruit, a brown basket, Score: 0, and Lives: 3." width="100%"}
![Catch the Fruit in Chrome after one successful catch.](../figures/chapter_10/fruit-catch.png){#fig-ch12-fruit-catch fig-alt="The Catch the Fruit page shows Score: 1 and Lives: 3 after a fruit lands in the basket." width="100%"}
![Catch the Fruit in Chrome after three missed fruit end the game.](../figures/chapter_10/fruit-game-over.png){#fig-ch12-fruit-over fig-alt="The Catch the Fruit page shows Game over! Score: 0 and Lives: 0." width="100%"}

**Read the pictures:** The six state values from the planning sketch control the game. The loop calls the planned update and draw jobs in order. A catch increases `score`; a miss decreases `lives`. When lives reach zero, `gameOver` stops the loop, and Restart restores the initial state.

::: {.callout-note .advanced-study title="Advanced Study | From one-file games to structured applications" icon="false" collapse="false"}

[OPTIONAL DEEPER DIVE]{.study-badge}

As games grow, split responsibilities. HTML defines interface elements, CSS defines appearance, and JavaScript controls behavior. JavaScript itself can be separated into modules such as `input.js`, `player.js`, `enemies.js`, and `game.js`. This is also the point where a library such as Phaser becomes useful.

```html
<script type="module" src="game.js"></script>
```

**Different files, different jobs.** HTML creates the interface, CSS controls appearance, and JavaScript reads input and changes state. Splitting files changes organization, not those responsibilities.

`type="module"` allows the entry script to use `import` and `export`. A path such as `./player.js` names an actual neighboring file, not a built-in browser feature.

Serve module-based projects through a local development server. Opening HTML directly with a `file://` address can cause module-loading restrictions. Earlier one-file examples do not need modules.

Further reading: [MDN: JavaScript modules](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Modules).

![The DOM is a tree of page elements JavaScript can read and change.](../figures/chapter_10/dom-tree.png){#fig-ch12 fig-alt="The document contains html, which contains head and body. Body contains a start button and a game canvas." width="100%"}

**Read the picture:** The browser keeps elements in a tree. `button#start` means a button with `id="start"`, while `canvas#game` means a canvas with `id="game"`. JavaScript can find those elements and connect them to game behavior.

:::
